In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Surah al-Mujadila (58)**

It is pronounced with a fatha or a kasra on the *dal*, and the second is the well-known form. It is also called *Surat Qad Sami'a* (the surah beginning with "Qad sami'a"). In the Mus'haf of Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him, it is called *al-Zihar* (the surah of Zihar, a pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband declared his wife forbidden to him by comparing her to his mother's back). According to what is narrated from Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, it is Medinan. Al-Kalbi and Ibn al-Sa'ib said it is Medinan except for the verse of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is the fourth of them﴾ [al-Mujadila: 7]. It is narrated from Ata': the first ten verses of it are Medinan and the rest are Meccan. This was reversed in the case of al-Baydawi, who said that it has twenty-one verses in the Meccan and the last Medinan reckoning, and twenty-two in the rest. In al-Taysir, it has twenty-four verses, and this differs from what is well known in the books on counting the verses.

The connection (*munasaba*) between it and what precedes it is that the previous surah ended with the grace (*fadl*) of Allah, the Exalted, and this one opens with something of that same kind. Some of the eminent scholars said about this: when the opening of the previous surah mentioned the sublime attributes of Allah, the Exalted, among which are *al-Zahir* (the Manifest) and *al-Batin* (the Hidden), and He, glorified is He, said: ﴿He knows what enters into the earth and what emerges from it, and what descends from the sky and what ascends into it. And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid: 4], this surah opens by mentioning that He, majestic and exalted is He, heard the speech of the woman who disputed (*al-mujadila*), who complained to Him, the Exalted. For this reason, 'A'isha said, as narrated by al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and al-Bukhari in a mu'allaq (suspended narration) form, when it was revealed: "Praise be to Allah, whose hearing encompasses all voices. The woman who disputed came to the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, speaking to him while I was in a corner of the house and could not hear what she was saying. So Allah, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿Allah has heard﴾ [al-Mujadila: 1]," and so on. After that, He, glorified is He, mentioned: ﴿Do you not see that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth? There is no secret conversation of three but that He is the fourth of them,﴾ and the verse continues. This is an elaboration of the general statement of His, the Exalted: ﴿And He is with you wherever you are.﴾ By this the wisdom of separating the two surahs is known, even though the Hadid and the Hashr are alike in beginning with *Sabbih* (glorifying), and other such points that are not hidden from the reflective.

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

﴿Qad sami'a Allah﴾ [Allah has indeed heard]: the *dal* is pronounced clearly (*idhhar*). Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Muhaysin read it with assimilation (*idgham*) of the *dal* into the *sin*. Khalaf ibn Hisham al-Bazzar said: "I heard al-Kisa'i say: whoever reads *qad sami'a* with the *dal* clearly, his tongue is non-Arab (a'jami), not Arabic." But this should not be paid attention to, for both ways are eloquent and transmitted with full certainty (*mutawatir*). Rather, the majority hold the clear pronunciation.

﴿The speech of she who disputes with you concerning her husband﴾: that is, she argues with you about the matter of her husband and what he had done to her by way of *zihar*. It is also read *tuhawiruka* (converses with you), and the meaning is as stated above. And *tuhawiluka* (questions you), that is, asks you.

﴿And complains to Allah﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) on *tujadiluka* (disputes with you), so the clause has no place in terms of *i'rab* (grammatical case-ending analysis). It has been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: she disputes with you while complaining of her condition to Allah, the Exalted. But this has a semantic remoteness. Even so, a subject (*mubtada'*) is supposed with it, meaning: "and she complains," because in eloquent usage the present-tense verb is not joined with the *waw*; so a subject is supposed with it to make it a nominal clause.

Her complaint to Allah is the display of her distress and of what she was harboring of grief and sorrow, and her humbling of herself before Him, majestic and exalted is He. It comes from *al-shakwa*, whose original sense is opening a *shakwa* (a small waterskin in which water is put) and displaying what is in it; then it spread to this usage.

She was a female Companion from the Ansar. Her name and her father's name are disputed. It was said: Khawla bint Tha'laba ibn Malik; and it was said: bint Khuwaylid; and it was said: bint Hakim; and it was said: bint al-Samit; and it was said: Khuwayla, in the diminutive, bint Tha'laba; and it was said: bint Malik ibn Tha'laba; and it was said: Jamila bint al-Samit; and it was said: other than that. Most of them hold that she was Khawla bint Tha'laba ibn Malik al-Khazrajiyya. Most narrators hold that the husband in this incident was Aws ibn al-Samit, brother of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit. It was said: he was Salama ibn Sakhr al-Ansari. The truth is that this has a different story.

**[Page 3]**

The verse was revealed concerning Khawla and her husband Aws. That is because her husband Aws was an elderly man whose temper had become bad. He entered upon her one day, she argued with him over something, and he became angry and said: "You are to me like the back of my mother." In the pre-Islamic period, when a man said this to his wife, she became forbidden to him. This was the first *zihar* in Islam. He regretted it immediately, and he called her, but she refused and said: "By Him in whose hand is Khawla's soul, you shall not approach me after you have said what you said, until Allah and His Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, judge concerning us." So she went to the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, Aws married me when I was young and desirable. But when my years advanced and my belly was emptied (i.e., my children multiplied), he made me like his mother to him, and left me for someone else. So if you find for me a concession, O Messenger of Allah, by which you revive me and him, then tell me of it." He, peace be upon him, said: "By Allah, I have not been commanded anything concerning your matter until now." In another narration: "I see you only as having become forbidden to him." She said: "He did not mention divorce." She argued with the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, many times, then she said: "O Allah, I complain to You of the severity of my loneliness and what grieves me of separation from him." In another narration she said: "I complain to Allah, the Exalted, of my poverty and the severity of my condition, and that I have young children; if I gather them to him they are lost, and if I gather them to me they go hungry." She began raising her head to the sky and saying: "O Allah, I complain to You, O Allah." So [the Prophet said]: "Send down (revelation) upon the tongue of Your Prophet." She had not left until the Qur'an was revealed concerning her. The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "O Khawla, rejoice!" She said: "Good?" Then he, peace be upon him, recited to her: ﴿Allah has indeed heard﴾ and the verses.

'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, used to honor her when she entered upon him and would say: "Allah, the Exalted, has indeed heard her."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated that she met him, may Allah be pleased with him, while he was walking with the people, and she stopped him. He stopped for her, came near her, lent her his ear, and placed his hand upon her shoulders until she finished her need and left. A man said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, you have detained the men of Quraysh for this old woman?" He said: "Woe to you! Do you know who this is?" He said: "No." He said: "This is a woman whose complaint Allah, the Exalted, heard from above the seven heavens. This is Khawla bint Tha'laba. By Allah, if she had not left until the night came, I would not have left until I had fulfilled her need." In a narration of al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, she said to him: "Stop, O 'Umar," and he stopped, and she spoke harshly to him. A man said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I have never seen the like of today!" He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "What prevents me from listening to her, when she is the one whom Allah, the Exalted, listened to, and revealed concerning her what He revealed: ﴿Allah has indeed heard﴾ and the verses?"

Hearing (*al-sama'*) is used metaphorically (*majaz*) for acceptance and response, by the relation of cause (*'alaqat al-sababiyya*), or it is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for that. The particle *qad* is for emphasis (*tahqiq*) or for anticipation (*tawaqqu'*). It refers to relieving the distress, not to hearing, because hearing is established; or it refers to hearing, because it is metaphorical or metonymic for acceptance. The intended meaning is that the addressee was anticipating that. The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, was anticipating that Allah, the Exalted, would reveal the ruling of the incident and relieve the one disputing of her distress, and the reports contain what indicates this.

As for the hearing in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah hears your conversation﴾, it is according to what is well known concerning it, namely that it is an attribute by which voices are perceived, distinct from the attribute of knowledge; or it is that it refers back to the attribute of knowledge. *Al-tahawur* (conversation) means the mutual speech in discourse. It has been permitted that it be meant as repeated speech, and it is said: "I spoke to him, but he did not return to me a *hiwar*, *hawir*, or *mahura*," meaning he did not answer me with anything. The present-tense form indicates the continuity of hearing according to the continuity and renewal of the conversation. Placing her within the same address by way of precedence (*taghlib*) is an honor to her from two aspects.

The clause is a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*) functioning as a reason (*ta'lil*) for what precedes it, for her persistent insistence on the matter, her exaggerated humbling before Allah, the Exalted, and his, peace be upon him, defending her, together with His, majestic and exalted is He, knowledge of their conditions, are among the reasons for answering. It has been said that it is a circumstantial clause like the preceding clause, but this too is remote.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing﴾ is a reason for what precedes it by way of affirmation: that is, He, exalted is He, hears all things heard and sees all things seen, in the most complete and perfect manner. Part of that necessity is that He, glorified is He, hears their conversation and sees what accompanies it of states, among which is her raising her head to the sky and all other effects of humbling. The Divine Name in both places is for inspiring awe, for giving the ruling a reason through the name Allah which is known for the attribute of divinity (*uluhiyya*), and for emphasizing the independence of the two clauses.

His saying, majestic and exalted is He:

[Page 5]

Those of you who liken their wives to their mothers' backs (﴿الَّذِينَ يُظاهِرُونَ مِنكم مِن نِسائِهِمْ﴾). This begins an explanation of the status of *zihar* (the pre-Islamic and Islamic form of divorce in which a husband likens his wife to a woman who is permanently forbidden to him, such as his mother) and the legal ruling that follows from it. It also establishes that the woman's supplication and complaint were accepted, by way of a new, independent statement.

*Zihar* linguistically is a verbal noun of *zahara*, which is of the pattern *mufa'alah* from *al-zahr* (back). It is used with various meanings, all related to the back, both in meaning and in form, according to the different purposes. One says: "Zayd *zahara* 'Amr," meaning he faced his back to 'Amr's back literally, and likewise if he angered him; and even if there is no literal facing, this is by way of consideration that angering him requires this facing. *Zahara* also means to help him, when he supports him, by way of consideration that one says "his back was strengthened" if he supported him. One says "he *tazahara* between two garments" when he wears one over the other, by way of considering that each of them makes the other a back for the garment. And one says "he *zahara* from his wife" when he says to her, "You are to me like the back of my mother." The most that can be said is that the word *zahr* (back) in some of these constructions is metaphorical, and that does not prevent deriving from it, and the derived form is also metaphorical. This last meaning is the one in which the verses were revealed.

The Hanafis defined it legally as likening a wife, or a part of her that represents the whole, such as the head, or a common portion of her such as one-third, to a close relative who is forbidden to him permanently, or to a limb of hers the viewing of which is forbidden to him.

It is reported from the Shafi'is that it is likening her, or a limb of hers, to someone forbidden to him by blood, by fosterage, or by marriage, or to a limb that is not mentioned for honor, such as the hand or the chest. Likewise, a limb that is mentioned for her, such as the eye or the head, counts if he intends the meaning of *zihar*, which is likening her to the prohibition of one such as the mother, and not if he intends honor, or if he is unspecific, according to the more correct view. Restricting the forbidden relative to the mother is an older opinion of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him. The details are in the jurisprudence books of both schools.

*Zihar*, in the sense described above, was a form of divorce in the pre-Islamic period, and it is said also in the early period of Islam.

Some scholars have reported that it was a divorce that entailed a permanent prohibition with no possibility of return. It has also been said that it was not a divorce in every respect, but rather left her suspended, neither a married woman nor free to marry another. Some eminent scholars mentioned that they regarded it as a divorce reinforced by an oath of abstention, and for this reason the Shafi'is said that it contains both aspects. The indication of its legal ruling will come later, God willing.

The verb is followed by *min* (from), although it can take a direct object, because it implies the meaning of distancing, and because, as you have heard, it was a divorce, and divorce involves distancing. As for the word "back" in the expression "You are to me like the back of my mother," it has been said to be metaphorical for the belly, since a man only mounts the belly, so "like the back of my mother" means "like her belly," by the relation of contiguity; and also because the back is the pillar of the body. But the obstacle that prevents the literal sense is not clear from the rhetorical considerations. It has also been said that the back was specified because it is the place of riding, and the woman is the husband's mount, and for this reason the thing ridden is called a back. It has also been said that this was specified because having intercourse with a woman from her back, through her front, was forbidden, so having intercourse with one's mother from her back is even more forbidden, and therefore the severity was increased.

The insertion of "from among you" (﴿مِنكُمْ﴾) in the verse is for depiction and reproach, because *zihar* was specific to the Arabs. From this it is known that it is not part of the concept of a qualifier (*mafhum al-sifah*), so that it could be used as evidence against the validity of *zihar* by a non-Muslim protected subject (*dhimmi*), as was reported from the Malikis. For this reason the Shafi'is said that it is valid from a *dhimmi* and from a non-combatant enemy (*harbi*), because of the generality of the verse. Likewise the Hanbalis and the Hanafis

[Page 5]

say that it is not valid from either of them. In a report from Abu Hanifa, its validity from a *dhimmi* is mentioned, but the relied-upon narration is that it is not valid, because he is not among those eligible for expiation (*kaffarah*). The Shafi'is were criticized for their claim that it is valid from him, given that they require intention for the expiation, and for the emancipation of a slave in the expiation for oaths, and given the impossibility of his owning a believing slave, because an unbeliever cannot own a believer. Some of their eminent scholars said that expiation contains an element of penalty, and intending it is disbelief if done by an unbeliever in manumission, for the purpose of distinguishing (the act), as in the payment of debts; but not fasting, because it is not valid from him, because it is a bodily act of worship which does not pass to feeding for him, since he is able to do it by becoming Muslim; if he is unable, it passes (to feeding), and he intends it for distinction too. It is conceivable that he owns (a slave) to a Muslim through an inheritance or the conversion of his slave, or he says to a Muslim, "Free your slave on my behalf as expiation," and he agrees. If none of these is possible for him, and he is one who makes *zihar* while wealthy, he is prevented from intercourse, since he is able to own (a slave) by becoming Muslim and then buying one. End of quotation.

In the book of some of the companions, such as *al-Bahr* and others, there is a discussion with the Shafi'is on this issue, containing refutation and affirmation, which is not free of some points. The reason for this is little following of the authoritative books of the Shafi'is.

The two Haram imams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi' al-Madani, or the Makkan and Madinan readers), together with Abu 'Amr, read *yazzahharuna* with doubled *zay* and *ha'* (the verb in the form *yazzahharuna*). Al-Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i) and Ibn 'Amir read *yuzahiruna* (the form *yuzahiru*, from *aza-hara*). Ubayy read *yatazahiruna* (the form *yatazahiru*, from *tazahara*). It is also reported from him *yatazahharuna* (from *tazahhara*). The relative pronoun (*alladhina*) is the subject, and its predicate is omitted, meaning "are mistaken"; its evidence, which is the words of God Most High, "their wives are not their mothers" (﴿ما هُنَّ أُمَّهاتِهِمْ﴾), is placed in its position. Or the predicate itself is this statement, meaning: "their wives are not their mothers in reality," so it is pure falsehood.

Al-Mufaddal reported from 'Asim the reading "*ummahatuhum*" with *damma*, in the dialect of Tamim. Ibn Mas'ud read "*bi-ummahatihim*" with an added *ba'*. Al-Zamakhshari said: "In the dialect of those who put the predicate in the accusative, that is, with *ma* (the negation particle), who are the Hijazis" — meaning that they are the ones who add the *ba'*, not the Tamimis. He followed in this Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. This was refuted, since the opposite has been heard, such as the verse of al-Farazdaq, who was a Tamimi:

By your life, Ma'n does not abandon his right, nor does Ma'n delay it, nor is he one who takes things lightly.

(﴿إنْ أُمَّهاتُهُمْ﴾) meaning: "Their mothers are not in reality" (﴿إلا اللائِي ولَدْنَهُمْ﴾), "none but those who bore them." Therefore no one is compared to them in prohibition except those whom God Most High added to them, such as wet-nurses and the wives of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so they entered into the rulings of mothers. As for wives, they are the furthest thing from motherhood. (﴿إنَّهم لَيَقُولُونَ مُنْكَرًا مِنَ القَوْلِ﴾) "Indeed they say an evil word," which the Law, reason, and nature also reject, as the indefiniteness suggests. The emphasis lies in its being "evil," since the saying itself from them is a certain fact (﴿وزُورًا﴾) "and a falsehood," meaning a lie, vain and turned away from the truth.

As for the reason why *zihar* is such according to those who consider it a false statement, on which the Lawgiver attached prohibition and expiation, it is clear. As for those who consider it a performative act that forbids enjoyment in law, like divorce, which is the apparent view, its basis is that this is by consideration of what it includes of placing the wife in the position of the mother, which contradicts the requirements of marriage. (﴿وإنَّ اللَّهَ لَعَفُوٌّ غَفُورٌ﴾) "Indeed God is Most Pardoning, Most Forgiving," meaning He is exceedingly pardoning and forgiving. He forgives what has passed of it and pardons the one who committed it, either absolutely or upon repentance.

It is known from the verses that *zihar* is forbidden. Indeed, they said it is a major sin, because it involves presuming to alter and change God Most High's ruling without His permission, and this is more serious than many major sins, since its consequence would be disbelief were it not that the belief is free of that, and the possibility that it is a likeness to such things. For this reason the Mighty and Majestic named it "an evil word and a falsehood." It has been mentioned by some Shafi'is that it is disliked to say "You are to me forbidden," because marriage and general prohibition can coexist, unlike with a prohibition resembling that of a mother. For this reason the great expiation (*kaffarah 'uzma*) is obligatory here.

Among them, according to what they say, the expiation of an oath is also (applicable)
