His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful (yuẓāhirūna, from ẓihār) and then retract what they said﴾, etc., is an elaboration of the ruling on ẓihār (the pre-Islamic practice of likening one's wife to one's mother's back, thereby declaring her unlawful to oneself), after the statement that it is a reprehensible matter, by way of a general legislation that organizes the ruling on this case in an initial manner. The relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl, "those who") is the subject (mubtada'), and His saying, ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾ (fataḥrīru raqabatin), is another subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "then upon them is the freeing of a neck." Or it is the agent of an omitted verb, meaning: "then freeing becomes obligatory for them." Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "so what is incumbent upon them is a 'freeing.'" On all three estimates, the sentence is the predicate of the relative clause, and the fa' (then) has entered it because the subject includes the meaning of a conditional. The mā (in limā qālū) is either a relative pronoun or a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyyah). The lām (in limā) is connected to ﴿yaʿūdūna﴾ (they return), which takes it just as it takes ilā (to) or fī (in). So there is no need to interpret it as one of these two, as some have done. Returning to what they said, according to the well-known view of the Ḥanafiyyah (the followers of Abū Ḥanīfah), is the intention to have intercourse. It is as if they understood "return" (al-ʿawd) figuratively as "remedying" (al-tadārruk), since remedying is one of the causes of returning to a thing. From this is the proverb: "The rain returned to what it had spoiled," meaning it remedied it through repair. So the meaning is: those who say that reprehensible saying and then remedy it, annulling it, which is the intention to have intercourse, then upon them is the freeing of a neck.

﴿Before they touch each other﴾ (min qabli an yatamāssā), meaning each of the one who makes the ẓihār and the one with whom it is made. As for tamāss (touching), it is said to be a metaphor (kināyah) for sexual intercourse (jimāʿ), so it is forbidden before the expiation, as the verse indicates. Likewise, its preliminaries (dawāʿī), such as kissing and the like, are forbidden according to us (the Ḥanafiyyah). It is said that this is the view of Mālik, al-Zuhrī, al-Awzāʿī, al-Nakhaʿī, and a report from Aḥmad, because the principle is that when something is forbidden, its preliminaries are forbidden, since the path to the forbidden is forbidden. This principle does not apply consistently to fasting and menstruation, because of how frequently they occur, so forbidding the preliminaries would lead to greater hardship. The scholar Ibn al-Humām said: "The verified view is that the preliminaries are explicitly prohibited in ẓihār, for there is no reason to read tamāss in the verse as a metaphor when the literal meaning is possible. Intercourse is forbidden because it is one of the instances of tamāss, like touching and kissing." Others said: "The kinds of sexual enjoyment are forbidden before the expiation, because of the general wording of tamāss, so it includes them by the indication of the text. The implication of the comparison in his saying 'like the back of my mother' is that the thing compared to, which is not lawful for enjoyment in any way, makes the thing compared likewise." According to the Shāfiʿiyyah (the followers of al-Shāfiʿī) too, intercourse before the expiation is forbidden. Likewise, touching and the like of every kind of intimate contact is forbidden, but not looking with desire, according to the more correct view, as in al-Muḥarrar. Imam al-Nawawī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The more correct view is permissibility, because the prohibition is not for a reason that undermines marriage, so it resembles menstruation. For this reason enjoyment is forbidden between the navel and the knee in that case." The complete discussion of this matter will come, Allah willing.

Al-Bayḍāwī related from Imam Abū Ḥanīfah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the annulment of the saying, which is meant by "return," is the permission of enjoying her in any way, even by a look with desire. He interpreted that as the permission of enjoying her by contact in some way short of counting it as permitted without contact.

Perhaps what is meant by "contact in some way" is contact that is not of the touching (tamāss) which they say is forbidden before the expiation. Whatever the case, the apparent linking of the ruling to the relative pronoun indicates that what is in the relative clause, namely the ẓihār and the return to it, is the cause (ʿillah). So these two are causes of the expiation, and this is one of the views on the question.

The scholar Ibn al-Humām said: "There is disagreement about the cause that makes it obligatory. Al-Nāfiʿ said: it becomes obligatory by the ẓihār and the return, because ẓihār is a major sin, so it is not fit to be a cause of expiation, since expiation is an act of worship (ʿibādah), or the part that predominates in it is the meaning of worship, and a prohibited thing cannot be a cause of worship. So he linked its obligation to both of them, so that the meaning of prohibition is lightened by considering the return, which is holding (the wife) honorably (imsāk bi-maʿrūf), so it falls between prohibition and permissibility. On this basis, it is fit to be a cause of expiation, which lies between worship and punishment. It was also said: the cause of its obligation is the return, and the ẓihār is its condition. The wording of the verse, namely what is mentioned, admits both, so it is possible that the ordering is upon both, or upon the latter. But when simplicity is possible, one should go to it, since it is the basic principle compared to compounding. For this reason, in al-Muḥīṭ it is said: the cause of its obligation is the intention to have intercourse, and the ẓihār is its condition." This is based on the view that what is meant by the return in the verse is the intention to have intercourse. It was objected: the ruling is repeated by the repetition of its cause, not its condition, and the expiation is repeated by the repetition of the ẓihār, not the intention. Many of our shaykhs held that it is the intention to permit intercourse, based on understanding a suppressed word (al-muḍāf) in the verse, meaning "they return to the opposite of what they said, or to remedy it." The same objection that applies to the previous view applies to this. The author of al-Mabsūṭ stated that by mere intention the expiation is not established: even if he divorces her or she dies after the intention, there is no expiation. This is evidence that it is not obligatory either by the ẓihār or by the return, for if it had been obligatory, it would not have dropped. Rather, the effect of ẓihār is the establishment of prohibition, so when he wants to lift it, the expiation becomes obligatory for lifting it, just as you would say to one who wants to pray a voluntary prayer: it is obligatory upon you, if you pray it, to first perform ablution. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that the supposition of a suppressed word is not fixed, based on what is related from many shaykhs. And the apparent meaning of the verse indicates causation, as we mentioned just now, and the one that makes the expiation obligatory is both of them together. This was explicitly stated by some Shāfiʿiyyah, who made this the analogy of the expiation for an oath. Then he said: "That does not preclude its obligation being immediate, although one of its two causes, namely the return, is not a sin, because when permissible and prohibited things are combined and their distinction is not possible, the prohibited is given precedence." The apparent statement of Imam al-Nawawī, may Allah have mercy on him, is that its cause is the ẓihār and the return is a condition of it, which is the reverse of what was related from al-Muḥīṭ. Then, whoever made the cause the intention meant by it the firm intention, so that if he intends and then it appears to him that he will not have intercourse with her, there is no expiation upon him, because the firm intention is absent; not that it became obligatory by the intention itself. Then it fell, as some of them said, because after it falls it does not return except by a new cause. Thus in al-Badāʾiʿ. Ibn Nujaym mentioned in al-Baḥr, from al-Tanqīḥ, that the cause of the expiation is that to which it is attributed, a matter that lies between prohibition and permissibility. Then he said: "That the expiation of ẓihār is like this according to the view of the one who made the cause compounded of ẓihār and return is clear, because ẓihār is prohibited and return is permitted, since it is holding (her) honorably and a breaking of falsehood."

As for the view that the thing added to, which is the ẓihār, is the cause (this is the view of the jurists of legal theory, al-Uṣūliyyūn), then its being between prohibition and permissibility, even though it is reprehensible speech and falsehood, on the consideration that the comparison may be for honor, so its being purely a crime is not settled. He then inferred that there is no benefit in the disagreement about its cause, giving the reason that they agreed that if he expedited it after the ẓihār and before the return, it is permitted; and if he repeated the ẓihār, the expiation is repeated even if the intention is not repeated; and if he intended and then abandoned it, there is no obligation; and if he intended and then divorced her irrevocably, it falls; and if he expedited it before the ẓihār, it is not valid. Then there is no impossibility in making sin a cause of an act of worship whose purpose is to expiate sin and remove the evil deed, especially when the meaning of deterrence in it is intended. What is impossible is to make it a cause of an act of worship that leads to Paradise. End of quotation. This is not free from good sense, except for his justification that ẓihār lies between prohibition and permissibility, for it is, as you see, not so.

Some of them interpreted "return" as "going back," and the lām as ʿan (from), as related from al-Farrāʾ, meaning: then they go back from what they said, so they intend intercourse. Al-Zayla'ī said: "This is a fine interpretation, because the ẓihār's effect is permanent prohibition, so when he intends to have intercourse with her and resolves on it, he has gone back from what he said." It is not hidden that making the lām mean ʿan is contrary to the apparent meaning. It was also said: "Return" means going back, and what is meant by "what they said" is what they forbade upon themselves by the word ẓihār, namely the touching, treating the saying as if it were the thing said, like what was mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We shall inherit from him what he says﴾ (Maryam 19:80). The meaning is: then they intend to return to touching, and there are two figurative usages in this. And from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, the meaning of ﴿then they return﴾ is then they regret and repent, that is, they resolve to repent. He seems to have understood "return" as "remedying," and the repentant one is one who remedies what proceeded from him by repentance.

It was objected: this implies that if he does not regret, the expiation is not obligatory upon him; and if the expiation is itself repentance, where is the meaning of "return"? Also, there is no sense in the speaker's saying: "then they resolve upon the expiation," then "freeing" etc. Return, according to the Shāfiʿiyyah, is realized in a non-time-limited (ghayr muwaqqat) and revocable (rajʿiyyah) ẓihār, by keeping her in marriage, even by ignorance or the like, after the completion of his ẓihār, even if it is repeated for emphasis, and after his knowledge of the existence of the condition in the conditional (muʿallaq) statement, even if he forgot or was insane at the time when it occurred, within a period in which separation is legally possible. So there is no return in the case of a menstruating woman except by holding her after her bleeding has stopped, because likening her to the forbidden requires separation from her; so by not doing it, he has become one who annuls it, remedying what he said. If separation by death, or annulment by something like apostasy before intercourse, or by irrevocable or revocable divorce, connects with the word of ẓihār, and he did not take her back, or he became insane or unconscious immediately after the utterance and did not keep her after recovering, then there is no return; the separation or its impossibility at first is also not a return, according to the more correct view, provided that the accusation (qadhf) and the lodging of a complaint with the judge about his ẓihār preceded it, according to the more correct view. If one who has made ẓihār with a woman takes her back revocably, or one who divorced her revocably immediately after the ẓihār, or one who apostatized and then embraced Islam immediately, while she has been had sexually, then the preferred view is that he returns by the revocation, because what is intended by it is the permission of intercourse, not by Islam, because what is intended by Islam is return to the true religion, and permission is something that follows from it, except if he keeps her after it for a period sufficient for separation. In a ẓihār that is time-limited, which occurs as he committed to, according to the sound view and a sound report concerning it, the more correct view is that the return is not achieved by holding her, but by intercourse that involves the penetration of the glans or its measure from its cut part, within the period, based also on the report, and because the permission is awaited after it. So holding her may be for awaiting it or for intercourse during it. Therefore holding is not established for the sake of intercourse except by intercourse during it, and so this is what achieves the return.

The objection to what they said is that "then" (thumma) indicates temporal delay, while the holding mentioned is immediately consequent, not delayed, so the conjunction should be with fa' (then, immediately), not thumma. It was answered that the period of holding extends, and in such a case the conjunction with thumma is permissible, while the conjunction with fa' is considered with respect to its beginning and its end. Based on this, there is no need to say that thumma is for indicating that the return is greater in consequence and graver in sin than the ẓihār itself, so that it may be said: this is not accepted. Nor is there need for the statement of the Imam that it is shared in obligation between the Shāfiʿiyyah and the Ḥanafiyyah, who say that return is the permission of enjoyment; this is rejected, because the permission mentioned immediately after ẓihār, as a verbal statement, is rare, so this does not apply to the Ḥanafiyyah.

It was also objected: ẓihār did not make the marriage contract prohibited, so that return would be holding her. From the Shāfiʿī reasoning mentioned earlier, what is in it is known. In the Tafrīʿ of Ibn al-Jallāb the Mālikī, it is related from Imam Mālik that concerning the meaning of return there are two reports: one, that it is the intention to keep her after ẓihār from her; and the other report, that it is the intention to have intercourse with her. Then he said: "Some of our companions said: return, in one of the two reports from Mālik, is intercourse itself. The correct view in my opinion is what I have presented." End quotation from his Mudawwanah.

[Page 9]

Ibn Hajar attributed the view that *zihar* (the pre-Islamic practice of a husband declaring his wife unlawful to himself by comparing her to his mother's back) means *al-'azm 'ala al-wat'* (resolving to have intercourse) to Imam Malik and Imam Ahmad. He attributed the view that it means the intercourse itself to Imam Abu Hanifa. He also mentioned that both are two opinions of Imam al-Shafi'i in his *qawl qadim* (earlier opinion). What he reported from Imam Abu Hanifa, however, none of his companions to our knowledge has reported from him. Al-Zayla'i reported it from Imam Malik, and no one else has reported it from him. Abu Hayyan in *al-Bahr* reported it from al-Hasan, Qatada, Tawus, al-Zuhri, and a group of others. He stated that it is one of two narrations from Malik, the second being that it means resolving to keep the wife and to have intercourse with her.

The proponent of the view that it means resolving to have intercourse was objected to by those who held otherwise, on the grounds that when the verse was revealed and the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered the one who had declared *zihar* to pay the expiation, he did not ask him whether he had had intercourse or had merely resolved to have it. The basic presumption is that this did not happen. Verbal events such as this are generalized by possibility, and they are explicit that the expiation is due before intercourse. So the return (*'awd*) would have preceded intercourse, and how then could it be intercourse itself?

The proponent of the view that it means resolving to have intercourse answered the question of why the Prophet did not ask by saying that the Prophet (ﷺ) already knew this from Khawla. Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi reported through the chain of Yusuf ibn Abd Allah ibn Salam, who said: Khawla bint Tha'laba told me, "It was about me and Aws ibn al-Samit that God Most High revealed the beginning of Surat al-Mujadila. I was with him, and he was an old man whose character had deteriorated. He came in to me one day and I argued with him about something, so he became angry and said, 'You are to me as my mother's back.' Then he went out and sat in his people's assembly for a while, then came back in to me, and there he was wanting me for himself. I said, 'Certainly not, by Him in whose hand is Khawla's soul, you shall not touch me after you have said what you said, until God Most High and His Messenger, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, judge concerning us.' Then I went to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and told him about this, and I did not leave until the Qur'an was revealed..." The report. The apparent meaning of her words, "I told him about that," is that she mentioned everything that had happened.

Among these events was Aws's desire to have intercourse with her, which is alluded to by "he was wanting me for himself." Her telling the Prophet (ﷺ) about this was more important to her than her telling Yusuf ibn Abd Allah ibn Salam.

It was answered on behalf of the proponent of the view that it means intercourse (regarding the latter point) that according to that proponent, the meaning of the verse refers to the time before *al-tamassu* (sexual contact) was made lawful by the Shari'a, and that intercourse was initially forbidden, which requires *al-tafkir* (the proper expiation or reprimand). This, as you see, is weak.

It is reported from al-Thawri and Mujahid that the meaning of the verse is: "Those whose custom it was to say this abominable statement and then cut it off with Islam, but then returned to the like of it, the expiation for the one who returns is to free a slave before the one who declared *zihar* has contact with her." They took *al-'awd* and *al-qawl* in their literal meanings. Then the consideration of custom indicates that the shift to the present tense in the verse means continuity in the past, time after time. They took the cutting off from the meaning of *thumma* (then), which implies delay, so that it would be valid in a way that does not require tying the obligation of expiation to the repetition of the word of *zihar*, as will come later, God willing.

It was objected to this that continuity contradicts cutting off. Furthermore, they had not cut it off with Islam, since the Shari'a had not yet prohibited it. The apparent sense of the sublime text is that it is *zihar* after Islam, because it is set down to explain its ruling, and the occasion of revelation fits this. It requires that the mere *zihar* without return should make expiation obligatory, which contradicts what the scholars of the great cities hold. It was answered regarding this last point that if these two are reported to have said that by way of personal reasoning (*ijtihad*), then their agreement with others is not required. This is explicitly stated in *Kitab al-Ahkam* and elsewhere. If nothing is reported from them except their interpretation of *al-'awd* in the verse as referring to what was indicated, then it is possible that they stipulated for the obligation of expiation something of what has passed, but they do not say that this is what is meant by *al-'awd* in it.

The People of the Literal Meaning (*Ahl al-Zahir*) said: the meaning is, "Those who say this abominable statement and then return to it, repeating it, by one of them saying, 'You are to me as my mother's back,' and then returning to it and saying it a second time, their expiation is freeing a slave..." etc. They also took *al-'awd* and *al-qawl* in their literal meanings.

This was also reported from Abu al-Aliya, Bukayr ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Ashajj and al-Farra'. Abu Hayyan also reported it as a narration from Imam Abu Hanifa, though none of his companions to our knowledge reported it from him. It was objected to that if this were intended, it would have said *yu'iduna lahu* (they repeat it), since that is more concise, and the word *thumma* would have no fitting placement. Moreover, there is no sound understanding in it from the standpoint of meaning. The revelation concerning it, namely the story of Khawla, refutes it, since repetition is not reported, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not ask about it. This refutation is strong.

As for what was said, that it was answered that it is possible that the understanding in it is that the phrase is not explicit in prohibition, so perhaps it slips from the tongue without intending its meaning. When he repeats it, it is definitely established that he intended it. The shift from *'anna lahu* to *lima qalu* (for what they said) is for the purpose of emphasis through explicit statement. The connection with *thumma* is for the distance in rank of the second and its remoteness from the first, because the second is what establishes the *zihar*.

As for al-Zayla'i's objection to this, that the wording does not bear it, since if that were intended it would say *yu'iduna al-qawl al-awwal* (they repeat the first statement), with *yu'idu* in the active voice from *al-i'adah* (repetition), not from *al-'awd* (return), this is ignorance arising from little familiarity with the speech of the eloquent and with their usage.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: the meaning of *'awd* is that he swears first to what he said of *zihar*, by saying, "By God, you are to me as my mother's back," and this is a return to what he said and a repetition of it in meaning, because the oath, being an emphasis of what is sworn to, conveys this. Therefore the expiation does not become obligatory for *zihar* without an oath according to him. This view nullifies *zihar* in meaning, because the expiation is for swearing about a matter in which he was lying. Also, the revelation concerning it refutes it, since no oath is reported, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not ask about it, and the presumption is its absence.

It was said: its *'awd* is repeating *zihar* in meaning, by saying, "You are to me as my mother's back if I do such and such," and then doing it, for he then breaks the oath and the expiation becomes obligatory. His doing that is counted as repeating *zihar*. But this is nothing, as is not hidden.

As for the suspension (*ta'liq*) of *zihar*, the Shafi'is mentioned that it is valid, because it is like divorce in requiring prohibition, and expiation is like an oath, and both are valid when suspended. So if he says, "If you enter the house, you are to me as my mother's back," and she enters, even while he is insane or forgetful, it is valid. But according to them there is no *'awd* in the assumed case until he holds her immediately after recovering or remembering and knowing that the condition has occurred, for the duration of the time needed to divorce her, and he does not divorce her. They have extended the discussion of the branches of suspension to what this place cannot contain.

According to us also, its suspension is valid, and likewise its restriction to a day or a month, and it does not remain after the period has passed. Yes, if he made *zihar* and made an exception for, say, Friday, it is not permitted. If he suspended *zihar* on a condition, then divorced her, then the condition occurred during her waiting period (*'iddah*), he does not become a *muzahir* (one who makes *zihar*), unlike a suspended irrevocable divorce, as explained in its proper place.

Al-Akhfash said: there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) in the verse, and its estimated form is: "Those who declare their women unlawful, then freeing a slave for what they said, then return to their women..." And no one goes to this except al-Akhfash, or al-A'sha, or al-A'mash.

In God's words, ﴿from their women﴾, there is evidence for us, and likewise for al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and a large group of the Companions and the Successors, may God be pleased with them all, that if a man makes *zihar* against his female slave, whether one he has had intercourse with or another, it is not valid. The explanation of this is that it includes our women and the slave-girl. Although it is linguistically valid to apply the word "our women" to her, the validity of the application does not require that it be literal, because the literal sense of attributing women to a man or men is achieved only with wives and not with slave-girls, since that is what is understood, so that it is correct to say, "These are his slave-girls, not his women."

The prohibition against the daughter of a slave-girl is not because her mother is intended by the text as one of "our women," but because she is someone with whom intercourse is lawful according to the majority. Without this restriction, according to us, even if *al-nisa'* (women) there were meant to include what makes the attribution valid, so that it covers both the literal meaning, namely wives, and the figurative meaning, namely slave-girls by the generality of metaphor, the ruling would be consensually established for slave-girls just as for wives. Here, however, there is no consensus, and no implication in our view either, so that it could be established by way of implication. This is because slave-girls are not in the status of wives, since lawfulness in them is a subordinate, unintended result of the contract or of ownership, so that these two would stand without it. This is not so in the case of a Magian slave-girl or a nursing slave-girl. By contrast, a marriage contract is not valid in a place that does not admit of lawfulness.

It was also argued that analogy, by its nature, does not require this comparison that is in *zihar* except for repentance, and the Shari'a came with establishing the prohibition in it regarding the one who has the right to enjoyment, and the slave-girl has no right in it, so it remains in her case according to the basis of analogy. And also that *zihar* was formerly a divorce, then it was transferred from that to a prohibition conditioned on expiation, and there is no divorce for a slave-girl. This is nothing to the discerning mind.

It is reported from Malik and al-Thawri that *zihar* is valid against a slave-girl without qualification. And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrima, Tawus and al-Zuhri that it is valid against one with whom intercourse has occurred. Furthermore, the condition is that she was a wife at the outset. So if he makes *zihar* against his wife who is a slave-girl, then he owns her, the *zihar* remains, and it is not lawful for him to have intercourse with her until he pays expiation, as they explicitly stated. By "wife" is meant a woman in a valid marriage against whom divorce can be pronounced. Therefore there is no difference between one who has been consummated and one who has not. So *zihar* is not valid from one who has been separated (*mubanah*), and of this is what you heard just now. Nor is it valid from a foreign woman (*ajnabiyya*), unless he attaches it to marriage, as when he says to her, "If I marry you, you are to me as my mother's back," and then marries her, in which case he becomes a *muzahir*.

Yes, in *al-Tatarkhaniyya*: if he says, "If I marry you, you are divorced," and then says, "If I marry you, you are to me as my mother's back," and then marries her, the divorce takes effect and the *zihar* is not binding according to Abu Hanifa. His two companions said both are binding. According to Malik, if he makes *zihar* against a foreign woman and then marries her, the *zihar* is binding, whether or not he attached it to marriage.

Some scholars said that the *zihar* of one who has not been consummated is not valid. Al-Muzani said that the *zihar* of a revocably divorced woman is not valid. The apparent meaning of ﴿those who declare [their wives] unlawful﴾ includes a slave (*'abd*), so his *zihar* is valid. Our companions mentioned that the *zihar* of a sane, adult, Muslim husband is valid, and a slave pays expiation by fasting. He does not pay it in a half amount (*la yunsaf*), because it contains the sense of worship, like fasting in Ramadan. Similar is one placed under restraint for prodigality, according to the two companions' view, which is the one given as the legal opinion.

Al-Tha'labi reported from Malik that the *zihar* of a slave is not valid, and that a woman does not enter this ruling. So if a woman makes *zihar* against her husband, nothing is binding, as is reported in *al-Tatarkhaniyya* from Abu Yusuf. Abu Hayyan said: al-Hasan ibn Ziyad said, "She becomes a *muzahira* (female one who makes *zihar*)." Al-Awza'i, Ata', Ishaq and Abu Yusuf said: if a woman says to her husband, "You are to me as the back of so-and-so," then it is an oath which she expiates. Al-Zuhri said: I see that she should pay the expiation for *zihar*, and this statement does not prevent her from her husband having intercourse with her. End.

The word *raqaba* (neck) for living beings is well known, and it is applied to a slave. This is from calling the whole by the name of a part, as in *al-Mughrib*, and this is what is meant here.

[Page 11]

In *al-Hidaya* it says: the "neck" (*raqaba*) is an expression for the person who is regarded in every respect (*al-dhat al-mar'uqa min kull wajh*). So freeing a slave in expiation (*kaffara*) is valid whether the slave is an unbeliever or a believer, male or female, adult or child, even a suckling infant, because the term applies to all of these. It follows from this that freeing an apostate (*murtadd*), male or female, a *musta'man* (a non-Muslim granted temporary safe conduct), or a *harbi* (a non-Muslim from the territory of war) is valid. In *al-Tatarkhaniyya* it says that freeing an apostate is permissible according to some shaykhs, and according to others it is not permissible, while freeing a female apostate is permissible without dispute, that is, because she is not put to death. In *al-Fath* it says that freeing a *harbi* in the territory of war does not count for expiation, but freeing a *musta'man* does count. In *al-Tatarkhaniyya* it says: if a man frees a *harbi* slave in the territory of war, then if he does not release him, it is not valid; if he does release him, there is a difference of opinion among the shaykhs, and some of them said: it is not valid.

The "neck" includes both the healthy and the sick, and each of them counts. In *al-Khaniyya* an exception is made for a sick person whose recovery is not expected, for it is not valid, because he is dead in legal terms (*hukman*). Regarding the freeing of one whose blood may lawfully be shed (*halal al-dam*), there is discussion. It is reported in *al-Bahr* that if a man frees a slave whose blood may lawfully be shed, and judgment has been passed for his blood and then he was pardoned, or if he had white eyes and the whiteness disappeared, or if he was an apostate and then became Muslim, it is not valid.

In *Jami' al-Fiqh* it says: a debtor (*al-madyun*), a pledged slave (*al-marhun*), and one whose blood may be shed are valid. Freeing a runaway slave (*al-aabiq*) is valid if it is known that he is alive. The "neck" must not be the woman against whom one has made *zihar* (the pre-Islamic formula of divorce by comparing one's wife to one's mother). This is because in *al-Zahiriyya* and *al-Tatarkhaniyya* it is stated: a female slave married to a man who made *zihar* against her, then he bought her and freed her, is it valid as expiation for his *zihar*? It is said that it is valid; it is also said that it is not valid, according to the opinion of Abu Hanifa and Muhammad, and differing from Abu Yusuf. Freeing a deaf person is valid by *istihsan* (juristic preference) if he is in such a state that he hears when called upon. In the report of *al-Nawadir* it is not valid. The blind person is not valid, nor is one whose two hands or two feet are cut off, and likewise one whose two thumbs are cut off, or one whose one hand and one foot are cut off on the same side. Also invalid is the insane person who does not understand. Freeing a *mudabbar* (a slave whose manumission is set for the owner's death) and an *umm walad* (a female slave who bore her master's child) is not valid, and likewise a *mukatab* (a slave who has contracted with his master for self-purchase) who has paid part of the price. If a man buys his father or his son intending the purchase as expiation, it counts for expiation. If he frees half of a jointly owned slave while being wealthy, and he guarantees the value of the remaining part, it is not valid according to Imam [Abu Hanifa], but it is valid according to his two companions. If he frees half of his slave for his expiation, then has intercourse, then frees the rest, it does not suffice according to him, because manumission is divisible according to him. A condition of manumission is that it be before touching (*al-masis*) according to the text, and the freeing of half took place after it. According to the two companions, freeing half is freeing the whole, so the whole was freed before touching.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, stipulated that the "neck" must be a believer, even if only by following a parent, a homeland, or a captor (*sabi*), by analogy of the absolute in this verse with the restricted in the verse about killing, on the common ground of the absence of permission in the cause (*'adam al-idhn fi al-sabab*).

The Hanafis said: the absolute is not to be interpreted by the restricted except in one ruling in one event, for in that case it necessarily follows by rational necessity, since a thing cannot be both required to come into existence absolutely and restrictedly, like fasting in the expiation for an oath. [The term] appears absolutely and restrictedly in the case of consecutiveness (*al-tatabu'*) in the well-known reading, which is permissible to recite, and the discussion of verifying this principle belongs in the principles of jurisprudence (*al-usul*).

They also said, on the assumption of descending to the Shafi'i principle of interpreting the absolute by the restricted in general: it does not follow that from restricting the greater matter, namely killing, there is the establishment of its like in what is lighter than it, so that the restriction in it would be an explanation of the absolute. What they mentioned as the common ground (*al-jami'*) is not sufficient. They agreed with [the Shafi'is] in much other than this, and differed in much as well. They said: it is required of the neck that it be free of a defect that impairs work and earning. Thus a child is valid, even one just born; a bald person is valid, and a lame person who can walk without a hardship that is not usually borne, continuously; and a one-eyed person whose sight in the good eye has not weakened so as to impair his work in a clear way; a deaf and mute person who understands the gestures of others and whom others understand by gesture in what he needs; and one with no nose, or no ears, or no toes, or no teeth; an impotent man (*'innin*), a castrated man (*majbub*), a woman without a vaginal opening (*ratqa'*), a woman with a blocked passage (*qarna'*), a leper (*abras*), a man with elephantiasis (*majdhum*), a person of weak grip, one who does not know a craft, a child of fornication, a fool (*ahmaq*), meaning one who puts a thing in other than its proper place while knowing its ugliness, a runaway slave, a usurped slave, and an absent slave whose life is known or whose state has become clear, even if his condition at the time of manumission is unknown for periods of time; a fetus, even if it is delivered less than six months after the manumission; one who has lost a hand or a foot, or one whose one limb is paralyzed, or one who has lost both the little finger and the ring finger of one hand, or two phalanges of the other [fingers], or the phalanx of a thumb, as al-Nawawi, may Allah have mercy on him, said. Nor is a decrepit person who is incapable, nor one who is insane for most of his time, nor a sick person whose illness is not expected to be cured at the time of manumission, such as one suffering from consumption (*sulal*). If he recovers after his manumission, the validity is clear according to the more correct view. Nor is one who has been brought forward for execution, unlike one whose execution has become obligatory for banditry before being brought before the imam. Buying or acquiring ownership of a close relative, ascendant or descendant, with the intention of expiation, is not valid; nor is freeing an *umm walad*, nor one who has a valid *kitaba* (contract of self-purchase) before he has been declared unable to pay. A *mudabbar* is valid, and one whose manumission is conditioned on a stipulation other than *tadbir*. They also said: if a poor man frees half of each of two slaves for his expiation, the more correct view is that it is valid if the remainder of both, or the remainder of one of them, is [free]... and so on.

Regarding the use of *fa* (then) in the words of the Most High: ﴿*fa-tahrir*﴾ ("then the freeing") etc., it indicates, as some eminent scholars said, that the obligation of freeing is repeated with the repetition of *zihar*. So if he has two wives, for example, and he makes *zihar* against each of them separately, he is obliged to two expiations.

In *al-Talwih* it says: if he makes *zihar* against his wife twice or three times in one session, or in separate sessions, he is obliged to one expiation for each *zihar*. There is an objection to this unqualified statement, for some have mentioned that if he intended emphasis in one session, it does not multiply. In *Sharh al-Wajiz* by al-Ghazali there is a summary of what it says: if he says to four wives, "You are to me like the back of my mother," if it is in one utterance, then there are two opinions; if it is with four words, then four expiations. If he repeats it, with one woman, then either he brings it in succession or not. In the first case, if he intended emphasis, then one; otherwise there are two opinions: the old opinion, which is also the view of Ahmad, is one, as if he repeated an oath on one thing; the new opinion is that it is multiple, which is also the view of Abu Hanifa and Malik. If they are not consecutive, or if he intended each repetition as a separate *zihar*, or he said it without intending emphasis, then each time is a *zihar* in itself. There is also an opinion that the second is not a *zihar* if he did not expiate for the first. If he says, "I intended to repeat the first," then there is difference of opinion, based on the principle that in general the meaning of *zihar* is divorce or oath, because it has resemblances of both. End of quotation.

The apparent sense of some expressions of our companions is that if he qualifies the *zihar* by a number, that number is taken into account. In *al-Tatarkhaniyya* it says: if he says to a non-related woman, "If I marry you, you are to me like the back of my mother a hundred times," then he is liable, that is, if he marries her, to one expiation for each.

The verse indicates that the mentioned expiation is before touching. If he touches her, he sins, and he should not return [to her] until he has expiated. Al-Bukhari... rather, the authors of the four *Sunan* reported from Ibn Abbas that a man, who was Salama ibn Sakhr al-Ansari, as in the hadith of Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and others, "made *zihar* against his wife, then had intercourse with her before he expiated. The Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: 'What prompted you to do that?' He said: 'I saw the anklet of her leg in the moonlight'—and in another wording, 'the whiteness of her shin.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'Then keep away from her until you have expiated.'" The wording of Ibn Majah is: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, laughed and commanded him not to approach her until he had expiated." Al-Tirmidhi said: a hadith that is *hasan sahih gharib*. Concerning its being sound, al-Mundhiri in his *Mukhtasar* rejected it, saying that al-Tirmidhi authenticated it, and its narrators are trustworthy, and it is well known that some of them heard from others.

[Page 13]

Al-Tirmidhi reported, and said: *hasan gharib*, from Ibn Ishaq, with the chain going back to Salama mentioned, "from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said, concerning one who has made *zihar* and has intercourse before he expiates: 'One expiation is binding on him.'" By this it is refuted against Mujahid in his saying: "another expiation is binding on him." This was reported from Amr ibn al-As, Qabisa, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Zuhri, and Qatada, and against the one who said: "three expiations are binding on him." This was reported from al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i. By this and by what preceded, there is a refutation of what has been said: that the expiation obligatory on him falls, and nothing is binding on him, and the prohibition of touching is not lifted except by it, not by ownership nor by a second husband. So even if he divorced her three times after the *zihar*, and she returned to him after another husband, or if she was a slave whom he came to own after he had made *zihar* against her, it is not lawful to approach her until he expiates. It is obligatory with latitude (*'ala al-tarakhi*), according to the sound view, because the command indicated by the verse is absolute, so that he does not sin by delaying from the first times when it is possible, and it is a performance (*ada'*) and not a making-up (*qada'*). It becomes specific at the end of his life, and he sins if he dies before performing it. It is not taken from his estate if he did not make a bequest, even if the heirs donate for the manumission; likewise for fasting it is not valid, as stated in *al-Bada'i'*. If he bequeaths it, it comes from one-third. In *al-Tatarkhaniyya* it says: if the one who wishes to expiate is sick and frees his slave as his expiation, and it does not come out of one-third of his property, and he dies from that illness, it is not valid as his expiation, even if the heirs permit it. If he recovers from his illness, it is valid. The woman has the right to demand from him intercourse and expiation, and it is incumbent upon her to prevent him from enjoying her until he expiates. The judge must compel him to expiate, to avert harm from her, by imprisonment; if he refuses, he is beaten. If he says, "I have expiated," he is believed, unless he is known among people as a liar.

This is it. Other matters remain, mentioned in the books of jurisprudence. "That" (*dhalikum*): the reference is to the ruling of expiation. The address is to the believers present at the revelation, or to them and to others of the community. ﴿*tu'azuna bihi*﴾ ("you are admonished by it"), that is, you are restrained by it from committing the forbidden, for penalties are deterrents from engaging in crimes. The purpose is to explain that the aim of legislating this ruling is not to put you in line for reward by your performing the freeing of a neck, which is a sign of a great reward, but rather it is to deter you and restrain you from committing what makes it obligatory. Thus in *al-Irshad*. This is clearly the view that expiation is a pure punishment; but it was previously stated that it is between worship and punishment. The words of al-Zayla'i indicate that the aspect of worship in it predominates. In *Sharh Minhaj al-Nawawi* by Ibn Hajar, in the book of *kaffarat al-zihar*, it says: expiation (*kaffara*) comes from *kufr*, which means concealment, because it conceals the sin by erasing it or lightening its guilt, based on the view that expiations are deterrents like discretionary punishments (*ta'zir*), or remedies for defects. Ibn Abd al-Salam preferred the second, because it is an act of worship, since it requires intention, so it is like the prostration of forgetfulness.

The difference between it—according to the second view—and burial of spittle (*al-dafn*), the expiation for spitting in the mosque, as established in that matter, is that burial removes the very substance by which the disobedience occurred, so nothing remains after it whose sin persists; unlike here, for expiation is not like that. According to the first view, what is erased is the right of Allah Most High insofar as it is His right. As for the aspect of the wrongdoing (*fisq*) resulting from its cause, repentance is necessary for it, like the case of the legal punishment (*hadd*). End.

When it is said that the manumission mentioned is an expiation (kaffarah), and that expiation covers the sin by erasing it or lightening its burden, then it is necessary that it entails a reward (thawab). That this is not counted as a reward is not free from scrutiny. Perhaps what is meant is that the greatest purpose of legislating this ruling is deterrence and restraint from committing what necessitates it, rather than exposing one to reward, though it may include reward in a general sense. Reflect on this. ﴿And Allah is All-Aware of what you do﴾ of deeds, such as the expiation and what necessitates it of the crime of zihar, ﴿Acquainted﴾, meaning: knowing their outward and inward aspects, and recompensing you for them. So be mindful of the limits of what He has prescribed for you, and do not violate any part of them.

[Page 14]

﴿Then whoever does not find [a slave to free], then [he must] fast for two consecutive months before the two of them touch one another.﴾

That is, whoever does not find a neck (a slave to free), then what is obligatory for him is fasting two consecutive months before the touching (tamassus). By "whoever does not find" is meant whoever does not own a slave, nor the price of one beyond what he needs for his sufficiency, because the amount needed for that is due to be spent (on necessities), so it is treated as if it were nonexistent. The amount sufficient in food for a craftsman is one day's food. For one who works, it is a month's food, according to what is in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Ra'iq). Whoever has a slave whom he needs for his service is considered one who finds (a slave), so fasting does not suffice for him. This differs from one who has a dwelling, because it is like his clothing and the clothing of his household.

According to the Shafi'is, the intended meaning is whoever does not own a slave or the price of one, beyond what each of them needs for himself and his dependents over the typical lifespan: maintenance, clothing, housing, and the furniture that is necessary, and beyond his debt, even if it is deferred.

They said: If the bondsman (qinn) or his price does not exceed what has been mentioned, because he needs him for service, for a position that requires that he not serve himself, or for a large (household) requirement in such a way that freeing him would cause him severe hardship that is not normally tolerated, and there is no consideration for the loss of comfort or for an illness he has or for his death, then there is no obligation to free (a slave) for him, because he is, by the law, one who does not have one, like someone who finds water but needs it because of thirst. Al-Layth also held that this (being in need) should be considered as not having one, like the one who finds the water mentioned.

According to our (Hanafi) school, the distinction, as al-Razi mentioned in Ahkam al-Qur'an, is that water is commanded to be kept for one's thirst, and using it is forbidden to him, unlike the servant. Wealth and poverty are considered at the time of expiation and of performing it, and Malik also said so. From al-Shafi'i there are several views regarding the time (of that consideration), the most apparent of which is what is our (Hanafi) view. They said: Because expiation, namely manumission, is an act of worship that has a substitute of a different kind, like wudu' and tayammum, standing and sitting in prayer, so the time of its performance is considered. The second view, as in the position of Ahmad and the Zahiris, gives precedence to the element of punishment, so the time of obligation is considered, as when a bondsman commits fornication and then is freed, he is punished with the hadd of a bondsman. The third is the stricter of (the view that it is considered) from the time of obligation to the time of performance. The fourth is the stricter of both of these, and he set aside what lies between them.

Whoever owns the price of a slave, but it is a debt owed by people: if he cannot collect it from his debtor, then he is one who does not find (a slave), so fasting suffices for him. If he can collect it, then he is one who finds (a slave), so fasting does not suffice for him. If he has wealth but a debt of similar amount is owed by him, then he is one who does not find (a slave) after settling the debt. As for before settling it, it is said he is also one who does not find, based on the view of Muhammad that it is lawful for him to receive charity, pointing to the fact that his wealth, because it is due to be spent on the debt, is treated as nonexistent in ruling. It is also said: he is one who finds (a slave), because the debtor's ownership of his wealth is complete, as evidenced by his being able to make all kinds of dispositions over it.

In al-Bada'i': If he owns a slave suitable for expiation, then it is obligatory on him to free her, whether or not he has a debt, because he is actually one who finds. The summary is that debt does not prevent freeing an existing slave, but it does prevent the obligation to buy one with what he has equal to the amount of the debt, according to one of the two views. The apparent position is that when buying becomes obligatory, the price of the equivalent is taken into account. This was stated explicitly by al-Nawawi and others among the Shafi'is, who said: buying a slave is not obligatory if it involves a loss, that is, an increase beyond the price of its equivalent, similar to what is mentioned regarding buying water for purification. The distinction between them by means of repetition is weak. According to the first view, as al-Adhra'i and others said, quoting al-Mawardi and adopting it, it is not permissible to switch to fasting, but he must be patient until he finds (a slave) at the price of the equivalent. Likewise, if his wealth is absent, he is required to be patient until it arrives. No consideration is given to the harm to them both from missing enjoyment during the period of patience, because he is the one who put himself into it. End of quote.

What they mentioned regarding the case where his wealth is absent agrees with our school in this regard. And if he owes two expiations of zihar (to two wives) and owns only one slave, and he fasts for the zihar of one of them, and then frees (a slave) for the zihar of the other: In al-Muhit, in a parallel case, it implies that fasting for the first is not valid. He said: he owes two expiations of oath (yamin). And if he has food sufficient for one of them, and he fasts for one of them, and then feeds (the poor) for the other, his fasting is not valid, because he fasted while he was able to make expiation with wealth, so it does not suffice for him.

The month is reckoned by the crescent, so there is no difference between a full month and a short one. Whoever fasts by the crescents, and it happens that each month is twenty-nine days, so that the total of the two months is fifty-eight, that suffices for him. If the crescent is obscured, then (each month is considered) thirty days, as in al-Muhit. If he fasts without the crescents, then sixty days are necessary, as in Fath al-Qadir.

The month is also reckoned by the crescent according to the Shafi'is. They said: If he begins in the middle of a month, then the month following it is counted by the crescent to complete it, and the first (part) of the third (month) is completed as thirty (days), because the crescent is impossible to observe in it, by combining it from two months. On this basis, it may coincide that his fasting is sixty or fifty-nine (days), and the first is not fixed, as is not hidden, so do not be heedless.

If he breaks a fast on one day of the two months, even the last, due to an excuse such as illness or travel, then it is obligatory to start over, because the consecutiveness is broken, and he is normally able to do it. Abu Hayyan said: If he breaks it due to an excuse such as travel, then Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, 'Ata', 'Amr ibn Dinar, al-Sha'bi, Malik, and al-Shafi'i in one of his two views said: he continues (building on what he has done). End of quote.

If he has intercourse during the two months with the wife he made zihar with, at night deliberately or during the day forgetfully, he must start the fast anew according to Abu Hanifah and Muhammad. Abu Yusuf said: he does not start anew, because it does not prevent consecutiveness, since the fast is not invalidated by it, and that is the condition. Their argument is that what is commanded is fasting two consecutive months in which there is no touching. So when he has intercourse with her during them, he has not performed what was commanded.

If he has intercourse with another wife, other than the one he made zihar with, forgetfully, he does not start anew according to the Imam (Abu Hanifah) as well, just as if he ate forgetfully, because the prohibition of eating and intercourse is only for the sake of fasting, so that the consecutiveness is not broken, and it is not broken by forgetfulness. Therefore there is no restarting. This differs from the prohibition on intercourse with the one he made zihar with, for that is not for the sake of fasting, but because it occurs before expiation, and the preceding of expiation before touching is a condition for its lawfulness. So by intercourse, forgetfully, in the course of it, the ruling of the preceding fasting is nullified concerning the expiation.

Furthermore, it follows that in the two months there must not be the fasting of Ramadan, because consecutiveness is stipulated in the text, and the month of Ramadan does not count as (fasting) for zihar, because that would nullify what God Most High has made obligatory. Also, there must not be in them the days on which fasting is forbidden, namely the two festival days and the days of tashriq, because fasting on them is deficient due to the prohibition against it, so it does not substitute for the complete obligation.

In al-Bahr: A traveler in Ramadan may fast for another obligation. Regarding the sick person, there are two narrations. Fasting specific days of vow during the course of the two months with the intention of expiation does not break consecutiveness. If someone is able to free a slave on the last day of the two months before sunset, it becomes obligatory for him to free (a slave), because what is intended is the continuation of not finding (a slave) until the completion of the two fasts; and his fasting at that point is voluntary. The better course is to complete that day, and if he breaks it, there is no makeup obligation on him, because he began it as one who is discharging (an obligation), not as one who is binding himself. This is contrary to Zufar.

In Tuhfat (al-Muhtaj) of the Shafi'is: If after fasting the two months it becomes clear that he had wealth which he inherited and he did not know of it, his fasting is not counted, according to the more correct view, taking into account what is actually the case, that is, he was one who finds (a slave) by that consideration. I do not recall the ruling on that among our companions. The apparent implication of what they mentioned regarding one who performed tayammum while there was water in his baggage that someone else had placed there, without his knowing of it, is that the validity of his tayammum allows the reckoning of the fasting here. The Shafi'is have explicitly stated, regarding one in whose baggage water was placed and who did not fall short in seeking it, or who had a well nearby whose traces were hidden, that his tayammum is not invalidated; so let the distinction between this case and that one be considered. Perhaps the reason is the stringency in the matter of expiation as opposed to tayammum, so let this be reviewed.

﴿And whoever is not able﴾ — that is, to fast two consecutive months. This is by not being able to fast at all, or by not being able to maintain its consecutiveness due to some reason, such as old age or an illness whose removal is not expected, as Ibn Hammam specified it with this. Others, and most of the Shafi'is, held this as well. The minority among them, such as the Imam and those who followed him, and which al-Nawawi affirmed in al-Rawdah, said: its continuation is taken into account in his estimation for a period of two months, based on the usual custom in such a case, or on the word of physicians. Ibn Hajar said: It appears that reliance on the word of one trustworthy physician among them is sufficient. The Shafi'is have explicitly stated that whoever is subject to severe hardship from fasting or from its consecutiveness, which is not normally tolerated, is not able, as it appears, even if it does not permit tayammum. Likewise, whoever fears an increase in illness.

In the hadith of Aws, as Abu Hayyan mentioned, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Are you able to fast two consecutive months?" He said: "By God, O Messenger of God, I, when I do not eat three times in a day and night, my sight weakens and I fear my eyes will be dimmed." — the report.

They counted among the causes of inability the shabaq, which is intense sexual desire.

It was cited as evidence for this what Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and others narrated from Salamah ibn Sakhr, who said: "I was a man who had been given more of the desire for women than anyone else. When Ramadan came, I made zihar against my wife until Ramadan would end, out of fear that I would be intimate with her at night. I would continue like that, and I would not be able to stop until the morning overtook me. Then one night, while she was serving me, something of her was revealed to me, so I pounced upon her..." — until he said — "...so I went out and came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed him of my news. He said: 'Is that you?' I said: 'It is I.' He said: 'Is that you?' I said: 'It is I, and here I am, so judge me by the judgment of God Most High, for I am patient for that.' He said: 'Free a slave.' I struck the side of my neck with my hand and said: 'No, by the One who sent you with the truth, I have not come to own anything other than her.' He said: 'Then fast two consecutive months.' I said: 'Has what befell me befallen me except through fasting?' He said: 'Then feed sixty poor persons.'" — the hadith.

By his saying, "Has what befell me befallen me," and so on, he indicated the intensity of his desire, which made him unable to fast two consecutive months. He was not excused from fasting Ramadan, as Ibn Hajar said, because there is no substitute for it. It is mentioned that the overwhelming of hunger is not an excuse initially, because at that point it is absent, so he is required to begin fasting; if he is then unable to continue, he breaks the fast and moves on to feeding (the poor). This differs from desire, because it exists at the time of beginning, so its possessor is included in the general meaning of God Most High's saying: ﴿And whoever is not able﴾.

﴿Then feeding sixty poor persons﴾ — for each poor person, half a sa' of wheat, or one sa' of dates or barley, or flour, each like its origin, and likewise sawiq (roasted flour), due to reports which Ibn al-Humam mentioned in Fath al-Qadir. The sa' is four mudd.

I need to be careful here: the passage is a long classical text, and the system instructions require a complete, faithful translation. Here is the translation.

The Shafi'is said: for each poor person, one mudd, because it is authentically reported in one narration; and in another narration, a sa' is authentically reported. The latter is to be understood as indicating the permissible minimum, which is compatible with the recommended (mandub) amount, since abrogation is impossible; so the reconciliation (jam') is achieved by what has been mentioned. It must be something that qualifies as fitr (the obligatory charity of Eid al-Fitr), namely from the staple food that is predominant in the region of the one paying the expiation, for most of the year, such as dried cheese (aqit), even if it is for a town-dweller (baladi). Therefore flour and the like, which do not suffice in fitr according to them, is not sufficient.

The position of Malik, as Abu Hayyan said, is one mudd and a third by the Prophetic mudd. Ibn Wahb narrated from him two mudds, and it was said: one mudd and two-thirds of a mudd; and it was said: whatever satisfies (yushbi'), without specification. According to us there is no difference between transferring ownership (tamlik) and permitting (ibahah). So if he provides lunch and dinner for the sixty, or provides lunch for them twice, or dinner for them likewise, or provides lunch and a pre-dawn meal (sahur) for them, or a pre-dawn meal for them twice, and satisfies them with wheat bread, barley or the like, such as sorghum, with condiment, it suffices, even if what they were satisfied with does not reach the quantity required for transfer of ownership. The sixty must be the same group: so if he provides lunch for sixty poor people and dinner for sixty others, it does not suffice unless he repeats lunch or dinner for one of the two groups. If he feeds one hundred and twenty poor people on one day, one satisfying meal each, it suffices only for half the feeding; but if he repeats it for sixty of them, it suffices.

The Shafi'is required transfer of ownership, by analogy with zakat and the charity of fitr. This is because transfer of ownership more effectively meets the need, so permission cannot take its place. We say: the text here stipulates feeding (it'am), which in its literal sense is enabling someone to eat; permission includes this just as transfer does. In zakat the term is "giving" (ita'), and in the charity of fitr it is "paying" (ada'); and these are, in literal sense, for transfer of ownership. So stated in al-Hidayah. The allamah Ibn al-Humam said: It cannot be said: they agree that transfer of ownership is permitted, so if the literal meaning of feeding is what is mentioned, it would be a shared (mushtarak) or generalized term, or [a term having] both a literal and a metaphorical meaning. For we say: permission of transfer according to us is by the indication of the text (dalalat al-nass), and an indication does not prevent acting on the literal meaning, as in the prohibition of insulting and striking together with saying "uff." Likewise here. Since the text specifies meeting the need for food, transfer of ownership, which is the cause for meeting all needs of which eating is one, is more permissible, for in that case it meets the need for eating and other needs.

Al-Wani mentioned that feeding (it'am) makes the other person a ta'im, i.e., one who eats, because the literal meaning of "taima'tu al-ta'am" is "I ate the food," and the hamza makes it transitive to a second object, i.e., "I made it (someone) eat." As for "aṭ'amtuka hadha al-ta'am" (I fed you this food), it is a gift and transfer of ownership by the context of the situation. They said: the rule is that if the second object is mentioned, it is for transfer of ownership; otherwise it is for permission. This is what is stated in the books of lexicography: that feeding means giving food, and it is more general than being transfer of ownership or permission. Thus, do not be heedless.

It is permissible to combine permission and transfer of ownership for some of the poor and not others, such as when he transfers ownership to thirty and feeds thirty with lunch and dinner. Likewise, to one man, in one of the two narrations, such as when he feeds him lunch and gives him one mudd.

If he gives one poor person sixty days' portion, it suffices. If he gives it to him in one day, it does not suffice except for that day, because the aim is to fill the need of the needy, and the need renews every day; so giving to him on the second day is like giving to him on another day. This is without disagreement in the case of permission. As for transfer of ownership from a single poor person in installments, it has been said: it does not suffice; and it has been said: it suffices, because the need for transfer of ownership may renew within a single day, unlike when one gives in a single payment, since distribution is obligatory by the text. The Shafi'is disagreed, saying: there must be giving to sixty poor persons literally, so giving to one person for sixty days does not suffice. This is the position of Malik. The sound position in the school of Ahmad, which is held by most scholars, is that since God specified sixty poor persons, and by the repetition of need in one poor person he does not become sixty, the reasoning that the aim is to fill the need of the needy, etc., nullifies the requirement of the text, so it is not permitted. Our school is more consistent with this principle, and therefore they said: giving a single poor person the allotment of sixty in one payment does not suffice, reasoning that distribution is required by the text; moreover, the distribution of payments is not explicitly stated, but is only an implied (iltizami) implication of the number of the poor. So the explicit mention of the number is more fitting, since it is what necessarily follows. The most that their statement gives is that by the renewal of need the poor person is renewed in ruling, so it becomes a multiplicity in ruling. Its completion depends on whether "sixty poor persons" in the verse is meant in the general sense, including sixty in reality or in ruling.

There is no doubt that this is a metaphor, so there is no recourse to its implication. If you say: what is the meaning by which the word becomes a metaphor and includes the multiplicity in ruling? I say: it is need, so "sixty poor persons" is a metaphor for sixty needs, which is more general than whether they are the needs of sixty or the needs of one if their recurrence is established. However, the apparent meaning is the counting of the counted, the persons of the poor, together with the rational consideration that number is intended for the blessing of the group, the inclusiveness of benefit, and the gathering of hearts in love and prayer. This is stated in Fath al-Qadir. It is a sound statement which shows the preference of the majority's position.

The Companions (Hanafis) held that it is not required that the type of the thing given be uniform for each of the poor persons. So if he gives one person some wheat and some barley, for example, it is permitted if the total is the required amount, such as giving a quarter sa' of wheat and half a sa' of barley. Such completion is permitted because the intended purpose is the same, namely feeding. It is not permitted to give the value of the required amount of something specified in the text, which is wheat, barley, flour of each, its sawiq, raisins and dates, if it is from another specified item, unless the amount given reaches the quantity legally determined. So if he gives half a sa' of dates worth half a sa' of wheat, it is not permitted. Rather, he must complete for those to whom he gave the prescribed amount of that same kind which he gave them; and if he does not find them in person, he begins again with others. From non-specified items, such as rice and lentils, it is permitted, as when he gives a quarter sa' of rice worth half a sa' of wheat, for example, because there is no consideration of the meaning of the text regarding specified items, and the consideration applies only to non-specified items. Al-Shafi'i's opposing view is reported, so giving value is not permitted according to him in any case.

In expiation, it is not permitted to give a poor person less than half a sa' of wheat, for example, only. In al-Tatarkhaniyya: if he gives sixty poor persons, each one mudd of wheat, it does not suffice, and he must repeat another mudd for each. If he cannot find the first ones and gives sixty others, one mudd each, it does not suffice. If he gives each poor person one mudd, then they become wealthy, then they become poor again, and he gives each one mudd again, it does not suffice. Likewise, if he gives mudds to the mukatabin (slaves contracted for manumission), then they are returned to slavery, their masters become wealthy, then they are contracted again, and he gives to them again, it does not suffice, because they have come to a state in which giving expiation to them is not permitted, so they are like another kind.

Accordingly, "sixty poor persons" means sixty poor persons for whom nothing occurred during the feeding that contradicts this. The apparent meaning is that the agent of feeding is the one who made the zihar and is unable to fast. There is no difference between doing it himself or ordering another to do it. If he orders another and that person feeds, it suffices, because it is in meaning a loan (istiqraḍ): the poor person receives it first, then his ownership is confirmed, then he transfers it. By "poor person" (miskin) is meant one that includes the faqir. They said: the miskin and the faqir, when they are combined, are distinguished, and when distinguished, they are combined. It is required that the one fed not be his origin (asl), his branch (far'), his wife, his slave, or a Hashimi, for their greater nobility, so he is exempt from this lower status; nor a harbi (non-Muslim from enemy territory), even if a musta'man (one granted safe conduct), for their greater baseness, since they are not fit for even the least benefit. It is permitted that he be a dhimmi (non-Muslim under protection). If he gives by good-faith effort (taharri) and it turns out that the recipient is not eligible, it suffices according to the two (Abu Hanifa's companions), contrary to Abu Yusuf, as stated in al-Bada'i'.

The Shafi'is derived from the expression "not finding" at the point of transition to fasting, and "not being able" at the point of transition to feeding, that if he has wealth that is absent and he is waiting for it, he does not fast; and if he is ill with the hope of recovery, he feeds and does not wait for health in order to fast. This agrees with our school regarding fasting, but not regarding feeding, as you have heard. Furthermore, this ruling applies to free persons. As for a slave, it is not permitted for him except to fast, because he does not own, and even if he owns, emancipation and feeding require ownership. If his master frees on his behalf or feeds, it is not permitted, even by his command. It is obligatory to make feeding precede intercourse. If the one who made zihar approaches the wife during the feeding, he sins, but does not have to begin again, because God did not stipulate that it be before intercourse as He stipulated in the previous case. We do not carry the unrestricted (mutlaq) on the restricted (muqayyad), even if they are in one incident, after they have become two rulings. It has been said that the obligation was established only out of the supposition that expiation would occur after touching. The clarification is that if he becomes able to free a slave or fast during the feeding, or before it, he is obligated to expiate by what he is able to do. If it were permitted for one unable to do either to approach before feeding, and then he became able, it would necessitate that expiation by emancipation would occur after touching, and what leads to an impossibility is impossible.

It has been criticized: there is an issue with this, for the ability while the inability of poverty, old age, or an illness not hoped to be cured persists is a doubtful matter; and rulings are not established on the basis of doubtful matters at the outset; rather, only recommendation as a measure of caution is established. So it is better to derive the prohibition of touching before feeding for one who is obligated to expiate by what has come in the hadith: "Keep away from her until she expiates," and similar. The Shafi'is disagreed with the claim that if he becomes able to free a slave, for example, during feeding, he is obligated to expiate by it.

Ibn Hajar, may Allah have mercy on him, said: his ability to fast or to free a slave after feeding has no effect, even for one mudd, just as if he began fasting one day of the two months and then became able to free a slave. Some permitted touching during feeding without sin, and this is reported from Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him; and this is a misconception arising from his not requiring a restart. Al-Kashshaf explicitly states that for Abu Hanifa there is no difference among the three expiations in requiring that they precede touching, even though the verse omits mention of it at feeding, to indicate that if it occurs during feeding one does not restart, as one restarts fasting.

Some have made the mention of the condition in the earlier cases and its omission in feeding an evidence for Abu Hanifa's position of no restart, that is, with sin.

Ibn al-Munir criticized this in al-Intisaf: one may say to Abu Hanifa: if you make the benefit of mentioning the absence of touching in some of them, and dropping it from others, a distinction between their types, why did you make it effective in one of the two rulings and not the other? Is such specification not a kind of arbitrariness? Then he said: One may also say: we agree on equating the three in this ruling, namely the prohibition of touching before expiation, and the verse has articulated a distinction, so it is not possible to turn it toward what is agreed upon as equal; thus it must be turned toward the other. This is the limit of the inquiry with Abu Hanifa. He extended the discussion on this point in a manner that is not free of scrutiny according to the principles of the Imam.
