When the one who has performed *zihar* (the pre-Islamic divorce formula of likening one's wife to one's mother's back) is unable to do any of the options, the Shafi'is say: the obligation remains fixed in his liability. When he becomes able to perform one of the options, he does it. His ability to perform only part of a freeing of a slave or part of a fast has no effect, unlike part of the feeding of the poor. If he gives part of what is due to one of the poor, he gives that part, and then the remainder when he becomes well-off. The apparent view is that the prohibition on intimate contact remains until he has paid the expiation (*kaffarah*) in full. The harm to the woman from this is not considered, because becoming well-off is expected, like the removal of an illness that prevents intercourse. I have not reviewed the ruling on this matter in *zihar* according to the Hanafis. As for intercourse during the day in Ramadan, which requires expiation, Ibn al-Humam said, after quoting the hadith of the Bedouin who had intercourse with his wife and who was unable to perform the three options, and in which: ««The Prophet (ﷺ) was brought a basket containing dates, and he said: "Give this in charity." He said: "Is there anyone poorer than me, O Messenger of Allah? By Allah, between its two lava plains there is no household poorer than my household." The Prophet (ﷺ) laughed until his back teeth showed, then said: "Take it and feed it to your family."»» In a wording of Abu Dawud, with the addition of al-Zuhri: this was only a concession specific to him. If a man were to do that today, he would have no alternative but to make expiation. Most scholars agree with this position. Al-Nawawi, in his commentary on Sahih Muslim, mentioned that al-Shafi'i has two opinions regarding this incapable person. One is that nothing is required of him, and he argued for it with the hadith of the Bedouin mentioned above, because the Prophet (ﷺ) did not tell him that the expiation was fixed in his liability, but rather permitted him to feed his dependents. The second, which is the sound view according to our companions and the preferred one, is that the expiation is not dropped but remains fixed in his liability until he is able to pay it, by analogy with all other debts, rights and obligations, such as the compensation for game hunted during the pilgrimage and others. As for the hadith, it contains no denial that the expiation remains fixed. Rather, it contains evidence that it remains fixed, because he informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of his inability to perform the options, and then the Prophet (ﷺ) was brought a basket of dates and ordered him to give it as part of the expiation. If the expiation were dropped by inability, nothing would be owed by him, and he would not have been ordered to give it. This shows that it remains fixed in his liability. He was only permitted to feed his dependents because he was in need of spending on them at present, and the expiation is obligatory with flexibility as to timing. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not explain that it remained in his liability because delaying an explanation until the time of need is permissible according to the majority of the jurists of legal theory (*usuliyyun*). This is the correct understanding of the meaning of the hadith. The ruling on the matter has other opinions and interpretations, which are weak. End.

Some people said: there was no delay of explanation; rather, the Prophet (ﷺ) was content with the Bedouin's understanding without explicitly telling him that the obligation remained. Reports about the occurrence of such a case for one who has performed *zihar* are inconsistent, as is not hidden from one who consults *al-Durr al-Manthur* of al-Suyuti.

The issues of *zihar* are numerous and the positions on them vary. Whoever wishes full knowledge should consult the books of *furu'* (positive law). Were it not for following some of the great scholars, we would not have mentioned any of them. Nevertheless, most of this has some connection to the interpretation of the verse. And God knows best.

﴿That﴾ refers to what has preceded of clarification and instruction. Its position is either nominative as the subject of a sentence, or accusative with an implied verb governed by what follows, meaning: that is occurring, or: We have done that, ﴿so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾, and act by His laws that He has prescribed for you, and abandon what you were upon in your ignorance. ﴿And these﴾ rulings mentioned are ﴿the limits of Allah﴾, which it is not permissible to transgress, so adhere to them and stop at them. ﴿And for the disbelievers﴾, meaning those who transgress them and do not act by them, ﴿is a painful punishment﴾ for their disbelief. The term "disbeliever" was applied to the transgressor of the limits as a strengthening of the rebuke, and a parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need from the worlds﴾ (Aal Imran: 97).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 58, verse 5:

﴿Indeed, those who oppose God and His Messenger﴾ means: those who are hostile to them both and act in opposition to them, because each of the two opponents is in a limit and direction different from the other's limit and direction, just as each of them is on a side and a flank different from the other's side and flank. It was also said that the use of this term for the two opponents is based on the use of iron (ḥadīd), because of the frequency of fighting between them with iron, such as swords, arrowheads and other weapons. The first explanation is more apparent. Mentioning *muḥādda* (opposition) within the context of God's limits (ḥudūd Allāh), rather than *mu'āda* (enmity) or *mushāqqa* (defiance), has a fine effect that goes beyond the limit. Nasir al-Din al-Bayḍawi said: "Or they establish or choose limits other than the limits of God the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ)." Its connection to what comes before it is entirely clear.

Mawla Shaykh al-Islam Sa'd Allah Jabali said: "On this basis, there is a great threat in it for kings and evil rulers who establish matters contrary to what the Law (al-Shar') has defined, and who call them *al-yasa* and *al-qanun* (the law). And God the Exalted is the One sought for help regarding what they describe." End of quote. Shihab al-Din al-Khafaji, after quoting him, said: "The gnostic in God, Shaykh Baha' al-Din, may God sanctify his spirit, wrote a treatise on the disbelief of one who says: 'One acts by the *qanun* and by the Shari'a if one compares between them.' God the Exalted has said: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3]. Religion has reached a degree of perfection that does not accept completion. I wish I had seen this treatise and become acquainted with its contents, for unrestricted use of the word "disbelief" is problematic in my view. So consider this carefully. Then, there is no doubt that there is no harm in political regulations (al-qawanin al-siyasiyya) when they arise by agreement of the people of opinion among the People of Binding and Loosing (ahl al-hall wa-al-'aqd) in a manner that makes orderly organization good and sets right the affairs of the elite and the common people. Among them is the determination of degrees of discipline and deterrence for sins and crimes for which the Lawgiver did not state a specific prescribed penalty (ḥadd), but rather delegated the matter in that regard to the judgment of the Imam. Such a thing is not opposition to God the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ) in any way; rather, it involves fulfilling God's right in the most complete manner, due to the deterrence from sins it contains, and this is an important matter for the Lawgiver, upon him be prayers and peace.

What points to this is what is in *Tuhfat al-Muhtaj* (The Gift of the Needy): that the Imam may execute discretionary punishment (ta'zir) even if the rights-holder pardons, because what is dropped by pardon is the right of the human being, while what the Imam executes is the right of God the Exalted, for the sake of public interest. In *Kitab al-Kharaj* (The Book of Land Tax) by Imam Abu Yusuf, may God have mercy on him, there is also an allusion to this. The saying of God the Exalted, ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3], and similar verses, do not contradict this, because what is meant is the completion of religion in terms of its including what indicates God the Exalted's ruling, whether specifically or generally. What points to this is that no one among the mujtahids (qualified jurists) is criticized when he says something that was not explicitly stated in a specific text, and among this is what is established by analogy (qiyas) in its various types. Yes, the law that lies beyond this, such that it collides with what the glorious Shari'a has declared and deviates from the straight path, has in it what it has, as will not be hidden from the perceptive knower. It may also be said regarding the verse, on the meaning that al-Bayḍawi mentioned, that what is meant by the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, i.e., "those who") are those who establish the limits and laws of disbelief, like the leaders of disbelief, or those who choose them and act upon them, like their followers.

Then, the verse, according to *al-Bahr* (the Ocean of tafsir), was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh. ﴿Will be humiliated (kubitu)﴾, meaning: they will be disgraced, as Qatada said; or they will be enraged, as al-Farra' said; or they will be turned back in failure, as Ibn Zayd said; or they will be destroyed, as Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash said.

﴿except that He is with them﴾, knowing what passes between them ﴿wherever they are﴾ of places, even if they are in the belly of the earth, for His knowledge of things is not due to physical nearness, such that it would vary with the difference of places in nearness and distance.

Regarding the reason for specifying three and five, there are two views. The first is that some of the hypocrites stayed behind to hold secret talks, out of spite toward the believers, in these two numbers, three and five. So it was said: no secret talk of them is of three or five as you see them talking secretly like that, nor less than their number, nor more, except that Allah, exalted is He, is with them, knowing what they say. So the verse is an allusion to what was actually happening. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed concerning Rabi'a and Ḥabib, the two sons of 'Amr, and Ṣafwān ibn Umayya, who were one day talking. One of them said: "Do you think that Allah knows what we say?" The other said: "He knows some of it and does not know some of it." The third said: "If He knows some of it, then He knows all of it." That is, because whoever knows some things without a cause has known all of them, since His being knowing without a cause is established for Him with every known thing.

The second view is that it intended to mention the customary numbers of the people of secret talk and of those sitting in private for consultation (shūrā), and those delegated for that, who are only a select group of people of intellect and sound judgment. Their least number is two and upward, to five, to six, to whatever the situation requires and what sound judgment dictates. So He, mighty and majestic, mentioned three and five, and He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿nor less than that﴾, which indicates two and four, and He said: ﴿nor more﴾, which indicates what follows this number and is close to it. Thus in al-Kashshaf.

In al-Kashf, in the summary of the second view: the two numbers were singled out according to what is customary among the numbers of the people of secret talk, for they are usually few in number. So it was necessary to single out by mention numbers such as three and four up to eight and nine. Three was chosen so that His words, exalted is He, ﴿nor less than that﴾ would indicate what is below it, since if four and six, for example, had been chosen, then the lesser would be three and not two, except by extension. When these were chosen, five was mentioned to harmonize the two odd numbers. The matter revolved between three and five, and four and six, so these two were chosen explicitly for that reason. And because He, exalted is He, is odd (witr) and loves the odd. End of quotation.

It may be said: secret talk usually occurs for consultation, and that cannot happen except among a number, and the people of consultation are usually few in number. The more fitting is that it be an odd number of the numbers, such as three, five, seven and nine, so that when they disagree there is a side that is favored by the addition over the other side, and so one returns to it rather than the other, as is the custom today when people of consultation disagree.

'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, made the consultation committee six, because the matter was confined to them, as his words to them indicate: "I looked and found you to be the leaders and chiefs of the people, and this matter is only for you. Yet despite this, he commanded his son 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, to attend with them, even though he had no share in the matter of the caliphate. So after considering what has been mentioned of the oddness and smallness of the number, the matter revolved between three, five, seven and nine. Three was chosen because it is the first of the odd numbers, and when multiplied by itself it reaches its limit in the units, and no possible consideration is free of it, until

Al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 58, verse 7:

Allah, exalted is He, has begun in these verses with knowledge, when He said, glorified is He: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah knows﴾ etc., and He, mighty and exalted, has also concluded with knowledge, when Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿that Allah﴾ etc. From here, most of the early scholars (salaf) said, regarding what is mentioned in the midst of His saying, mighty and majestic is He: "the fourth of them, nor the sixth of them, and He is with them" that the intended meaning is His being so in terms of knowledge, although they are among those whose wording is not interpreted (ta'wil). It seems they did not count this as ta'wil, because its meaning is so evident and it is surrounded by what indicates it with a clarity that leaves no obscurity. It is known from this that what is widely held, namely that the salaf do not interpret, is not absolute in its application.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 58, verse 8:**

﴿Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret conferring, and then return to what they were forbidden from?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: It was revealed concerning the Jews and the hypocrites. They would confer secretly apart from the believers, look at them, and wink at one another about them, giving them to understand that some harm had befallen their relatives. They would continue doing this until the believers' relatives came forward. When this happened often from them, the believers complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he forbade them from conferring secretly apart from the believers. But they returned to the same behaviour. Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning the Jews.
[Page 26]

Ibn al-Sa'ib said: It was concerning the hypocrites. The address is to the Messenger (peace be upon him), and the interrogative hamzah (the letter alif-hamzah used for asking questions) is for expressing wonder at their condition. The use of the present tense (mudari') indicates the recurrence and renewal of their returning, and the bringing to mind of its astonishing form. Allah's words, ﴿and they confer with sin and enmity and disobedience to the Messenger﴾, are conjoined to what precedes and fall under its ruling, meaning: they confer about what is sinful in itself, a burden upon themselves, an aggression against the believers, and a mutual agreement to oppose the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He mentioned him (peace be upon him) by the title of messengerhood between the two addresses directed to him (ﷺ), in order to increase the censure of them and magnify the gravity of their disobedience.

Hamzah, Talhah, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab and Duways read ﴿yantajuna﴾ with a sukun-nun after the ya' and a damma on the jim, the present tense of intaja. Abu Haywah read ﴿al-'idwan﴾ with a kasrah on the 'ayn wherever it occurs. It was also read ﴿ma'siyyat﴾ in the plural, and it is later attributed to al-Dahhak. ﴿And when they come to you, they greet you with what Allah has not greeted you with﴾. It is authentically related from the narrations of al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from A'ishah: "Some Jews entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'As-sam 'alayka, O Abu al-Qasim.' The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Wa 'alaykum.' A'ishah said: 'I said: "Alaykumu as-sam, and may Allah curse you and be angry with you."' And in another narration: '"Alaykumu as-sam, adh-dhamm and al-la'nah (curse)." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "O A'ishah, Allah does not love the obscene or the one who uses obscenity." I said: "Do you not hear them saying as-sam?" The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Did you not hear me say: wa 'alaykum?"' Then Allah revealed ﴿And when they come to you﴾..." the verse.

Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (the Branches of Faith) recorded with a good chain: "From Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Jews used to say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), 'Sam 'alayka,' intending by it to revile him. Then they would say to themselves: 'Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?' So this verse was revealed: ﴿And when they come to you﴾, etc."

As for as-sam: Ibn al-Athir said: The well-known form of it is without hamzah, and they mean by it death. It has also come in a narration with hamzah, and its meaning is that you become weary of your religion (sa'imtum). Al-Khafaji stated explicitly that it means death and is Hebrew, and he did not mention the hamzah or its omission.

Al-Tabarsi said: Whoever says that as-sam means death, it is from sa'ama al-hayat (to be weary of life) by its going away, and this is a reference of it to the form with hamzah.

Al-Baydawi made the greeting by which Allah did not greet him (peace be upon him) to be their greeting to him with "an'im sabahan" (may you have a pleasant morning), which is a greeting of the Jahiliyyah, like "in'im sabahan." We have not found a report on this matter. Allah's words, ﴿and they say among themselves﴾, mean among themselves, and it is permissible to keep it on its apparent sense. ﴿Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?﴾, meaning: why does Allah not punish us for this—if Muhammad (ﷺ) were a prophet? That is, if he were a prophet, Allah would punish us for what we say of the greeting. This is more fitting for the first meaning, because "an'im sabahan" is a supplication for good, and turning from it to the greeting of Islam, with which Allah greeted His Messenger (ﷺ), and which is indicated by Allah's words: ﴿And peace upon the messengers﴾ [al-Saffat: 181] and ﴿Peace upon His servants whom He has chosen﴾ [al-Naml: 59], and what is in the tashahhud, "as-salamu 'alayka ayyuha an-Nabiyyu wa rahmatu Allahi wa barakatuh" (Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings), contains no great sin that would bring the expectation of worldly punishment, so much so that they say this and are not punished. Except if it is combined with it that they intended by it contempt and public display of disregard. Perhaps the one who says this is the hypocrites among the polytheists, and this is more apparent than that its speaker was the Jews. As for the ruling on greeting with it today: it is contrary to the Sunnah, and the view that it is disliked (makruh) is not far-fetched.

In Tuhfat al-Muhtaj (the Gift for the Needy): The one who initiates the greeting does not deserve a reply such as "sabbahaka Allahu bil-khayr" (may Allah greet you with good in the morning) or "qawwaka Allah" (may Allah strengthen you); his supplication for him in return is good, unless by neglecting him he intends to discipline him for abandoning the Sunnah of greeting. End of quote. And "an'im sabahan" is like "sabbahaka Allahu bil-khayr." The utmost that can be said in this matter is that it is a supplication that was used as a greeting in the Jahiliyyah.
[Page 27]

Yes, their greeting to him (peace be upon him) with it, in the manner they intended, is forbidden without any disagreement. ﴿Hell is sufficient for them﴾ as a punishment, ﴿which they will burn in﴾, meaning they will enter it, or they will suffer its heat, or they will be roasted by it.

﴿And wretched is the destination﴾, meaning: Hell.

﴿O you who have believed, when you confide in one another﴾ in your gatherings and in your private meetings.

﴿then do not confide in one another in sin and aggression and disobedience to the Messenger﴾ as the hypocrites do. So the address is to the sincere believers (al-khullas), with an allusion (ta'ridan) to the hypocrites. It is also permissible to take the address as directed at the hypocrites themselves, and they are called believers in view of the outward appearance of their conditions.

The Kufans, al-A'mash, Abu Haywa and Ruways read ﴿فَلا تَنْتَجُوا﴾ (fa-la tantaju), the present tense of intaja. Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿فَلا تَناجَوْا﴾ (fa-la tanajaw) with the assimilation (idgham) of the second ta' into the first. It is also reported that one of the two ta's is elided.

﴿but confide in one another in righteousness and piety﴾, that is, in what includes the good report of the believers and guarding oneself against disobedience to the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿And fear God﴾ in what you do and what you leave undone, ﴿to whom﴾ alone, and not to any other, glorified is He, whether independently or in association, ﴿you will be gathered﴾, and He will then requite you for that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 58, verse 10:

﴿Secret counsel is only from Satan﴾ — the well-known secret conferring, which is consultation concerning sin, transgression and disobedience — ﴿from Satan﴾, not from anyone else, in view of the fact that he is the one who adorns it and drives people to it. The words of the Exalted, ﴿so that he may grieve those who believe﴾, are another statement, meaning: it is only so that he may grieve the believers by making them imagine that some calamity has befallen them. It has been read as «liyahzana» (with a fatha on the ya and the za), in which case ﴿alladhina﴾ is the subject. ﴿But it cannot harm them﴾, that is, neither Satan nor the secret conferring can harm the believers ﴿in any way﴾ among things, or any measure of harm ﴿except by the permission of Allah﴾, that is, except by His will and decree, Mighty and Majestic is He, and that by His Glorified Self decreeing death or defeat upon their relatives. ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾, and let them not mind their secret talk.

The summary of this is that whatever the hypocrites confer about that which grieves the believers, if it occurs, it occurs by the will and decree of Allah the Exalted, in which they have no part. So the believers should not be concerned with their secret talk, but should rely upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and not grieve over it. This statement serves to remove their grief. From this it follows that the suggestion of al-Zamakhshari, that the pronoun in «laysa bi-darrihim» may refer to the grief, is weak. It is answered that the intended meaning is achieved on that reading too, for if it is said that this grief will not harm them except by the will of Allah the Exalted, their grief is dispelled.

Here also is a strange opinion: that the verse was revealed concerning the dreams which a believer sees in sleep that distress him and cause him grief, so that they are like a secret conversation conducted with him. But this, for all its problems, does not suit the preceding context or the flow of the discourse, as is not hidden. Furthermore, secret conferring among believers may itself be forbidden. Al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud have related from Ibn Mas'ud that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you are three, let not two of them confer apart from the third until you mix with the people, because that would grieve him." Similar to secret conferring in this regard is two people speaking in the presence of a third in a language the third does not understand, if that grieves him.

[Page 28]

When Allah, glorified is He, prohibited private consultation and whispering, it was understood from this that sitting with a gathering was also meant. So He, mighty and majestic, mentioned its etiquette afterward, by His words, mighty is the Speaker: ﴿O you who have believed, when it is said to you, "Make room in the assemblies," etc.﴾. When He, mighty and majestic, prohibited what causes hatred and aversion, He commanded what causes affection and harmony, meaning: if a speaker, whoever he may be, says to you, "Make room," then some of you should make room for others in the assemblies, and you should not crowd together in them. This is from their saying, "Make room for me" (ifsah 'anni), meaning "move aside." The apparent reading is that "in the assemblies" (fi al-majalis) is connected to "make room" (tafassahu). It was also said that it is connected to "it is said" (qila).

Al-Hasan, Dawud ibn Abi Hind, Qatada and Isa read "tafasahu" (with the verb in the form tafa'ala). The last two and 'Asim read "fi al-majalis" (in the plural). The majority read "fi al-majlis" (in the singular). It was said that the singular is used to denote the category (jins), in agreement with the plural reading. It was also said that it denotes a specific, known assembly (al-'ahd, a definite reference), and what is meant is the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The plural is used because it has multiple instances, according to the people who sat with him, peace be upon him, since each one had a place among them. In the reports about the occasion of revelation there is support for each view. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muqatil ibn Hayyan: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was on a Friday in the Suffa, and the place was crowded. The Prophet, peace be upon him, used to honor the people of Badr among the Emigrants and the Helpers. Some men from the people of Badr came, among them Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, and they had arrived before the others at the gatherings. They stood before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said, 'Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings.' The Prophet, peace be upon him, returned their greeting. Then they greeted the people, and they returned their greeting. Then they stood on their feet, waiting for room to be made for them, but the people did not make room for them. This grieved the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he said to some who were around him, 'Stand up, so-and-so, and so-and-so,' and he had a group stand up, equal in number to those who had come. This grieved them, and their dislike was seen on their faces. The hypocrites said, 'Muhammad has not been just in having those who took their seats stand up, and who loved to be close to him, in favor of those who were late in attending.' So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed this verse: ﴿O you who have believed﴾," etc. This happened among those who did not make room, out of rivalry for closeness to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and eagerness for it, and a soul hardly prefers another over itself in this matter.

Al-Hasan and Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: "The Companions used to compete for places in the battle lines when they were arranged for war, so none of them would make room for another, out of eagerness for martyrdom. So this was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed﴾," etc. Most scholars hold that it was revealed because of what the believers did of crowding together in his assembly, being stingy about closeness to him, and not making room for someone who came. Whichever occasion it was, the ruling applies generally: in his assembly, peace be upon him, in the battle ranks, and in other situations.

It was also read "fi al-majlas" (with a fatha on the lam). Either it is meant in the same sense as the kasra reading, and the fatha is an irregular reading (shadh) in usage; or it is meant as the verbal noun (masdar), and the prepositional phrase is connected to "make room" (tafassahu). That is, "If it is said to you, 'Make room in your sitting, and do not be cramped in it,'" ﴿so make room, and Allah will make room for you﴾, meaning in His mercy, or in your dwellings in Paradise, or in your graves, or in your chests, or in your provision. There are several opinions.

Some of them said: the meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, will make room for you in everything you wish to have room in, that is, of what has been mentioned and other things. You know that the meaning of "making room" varies according to what it is connected to, such as dwellings, provision, and the chest. So do not overlook this.

﴿And when it is said, "Rise up,"﴾ meaning, rise to make room for those who come. ﴿then rise up﴾, meaning stand up and do not hold back. Its root is from "nashz," which is a raised part of the ground, because the one who wants to make room for someone who comes rises upward, and so the place becomes wider. Or because standing up itself is a rising. Al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Dahhak said: the meaning is, when you are called to fighting, prayer, or obedience, then respond. It was also said: when you are called to rise from the assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ), then rise. This is because he, peace be upon him, sometimes preferred to be alone in matters of Islam, or to carry out duties specific to him, peace be upon him, which could not be accomplished or completed without being alone. The ruling was generalized, and it was said: if the host of a gathering says to those in his gathering, "Stand up," it is appropriate to comply. He may do so for a need, if it does not result in a greater harm than it. There is no dispute about its permissibility. Yes, a newcomer should not have someone removed so that he can sit in his place. Malik, al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man should not have another man removed from his place, but make room and widen the space."

Al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Talha and a group among the seven readers read "unshizu, fa-inshizu" with a kasra on the shin in both.

﴿Allah will raise those of you who have believed﴾: this is the answer to the command, as if it was said: if you rise, Allah, mighty and majestic, will raise the believers among you in the Hereafter, as a reward for complying,

[Page 29]

﴿and those who have been given knowledge﴾ of the Sharia, ﴿by degrees﴾, meaning many and exalted degrees, as the context indicates. The conjunction of "those who have been given knowledge" to "those who have believed" is a conjunction of the specific to the general, to honor them by treating them as if they were another category. For this reason the relative pronoun is repeated in the noble text. Al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud and al-Darimi narrated from Abu al-Darda', raised (to the Prophet): "The virtue of the scholar over the worshipper is like the virtue of the full moon over the rest of the stars."

Al-Darimi narrated from Umar ibn Kathir, from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever death comes to while he is seeking knowledge to revive Islam with it, between him and the prophets there is one degree." And from him (ﷺ): "Between the scholar and the worshipper there are a hundred degrees, between each two degrees is the distance a swift horse runs in seventy years." And from him, peace be upon him: "Three will intercede on the Day of Resurrection: the prophets, then the scholars, then the martyrs." So how great is a rank between prophethood and martyrdom, by the testimony of the truthful one who was believed, (ﷺ). And from Ibn Abbas: "Solomon, peace be upon him, was given the choice between knowledge, kingship, and wealth, and he chose knowledge, so Allah gave him kingship and wealth as a consequence of it."

And from al-Ahnaf: "The scholars nearly become lords." Every honor that is not established by knowledge ends in humiliation. And one of the wise said: "I wish I knew, what has the one who has attained knowledge lost, and what has the one who has lost knowledge attained?" The evidence for the virtue of knowledge and the scholars is more than can be counted. The most hopeful hadith to me regarding their virtue is what Imam Abu Hanifa narrated in his Musnad from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah will gather the scholars on the Day of Resurrection and say: 'I did not place My wisdom in your hearts except that I intended good for you. Go to Paradise, for I have forgiven you what you did.'"

Ilyas al-Kurani, the gnostic, mentioned that it is one of the hadiths of the chain of "first" (al-musalsal bil-awwaliyya), and the indication of the verse regarding their virtue is clear. Indeed, Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Allah, exalted is He, has not singled out the scholars in anything in the Qur'an as He singled them out in this verse: 'Allah has raised those who believed among you and those who were given knowledge by degrees' — Allah has favored those who believed and were given knowledge over those who believed and were not given knowledge, by degrees." Some scholars made the conjunction indicate difference in essence, by reading "those who have believed" as referring to those who believed and were not given knowledge. In another narration from him: "O you who have believed, understand the meaning of this verse, and let it encourage you to seek knowledge, for Allah raises the believer who has knowledge above the one who does not know."

Some have claimed that in his words, may Allah be pleased with him, there is an indication that "those who have been given" is the object (ma'mul) of an omitted verb, and that the conjunction is a conjunction of sentences. That is: "And Allah, exalted is He, raises especially those who have been given knowledge, by degrees." A similar statement was made by Ibn Abbas. Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Bayhaqi in al-Madkhal, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from him that he said regarding the verse: "Those among the believers who were given knowledge are raised by degrees above those who were not given knowledge."

Some verifiers said: there is no need to estimate an operative word, and the meaning is the same without estimation. Al-Tibi preferred the estimation and made "degrees" the object of that estimated verb, and he said: a lower-ranked matter that fits the context is implied, such as: "Allah raises those who believed in this world through victory and good remembrance, or He raises them in the Hereafter by sheltering them in what befits them of the chambers of the gardens, and He raises those who were given knowledge by degrees, as an honor to them." It is also permissible that the two relative clauses refer to one referent, and the conjunction is to treat the difference of attributes as the difference of essences. So the meaning is: Allah raises the believers who have knowledge by degrees. The conjunction being of the specific to the general is the more apparent view. Al-Intisaf said: the reward of raising degrees is appropriate to the action commanded, which is making room in assemblies and leaving aside what they competed for, namely sitting in the highest and nearest places to the Prophet (ﷺ). So when the one who complies with this lowers himself from what people compete for in rank, out of obedience and humility, he is rewarded for his humility by the raising of degrees, as in his saying: "Whoever humbles himself for the sake of Allah, Allah will raise him." Then, when He, glorified is He, knew that people of knowledge are such that they deserve, in their own estimation and in the estimation of people, the elevation of their gatherings, He singled them out for mention in the reward, so that it would be easy for them to leave aside the rank they have in the assembly, out of humility before Allah, mighty and majestic.

It was also said: He, exalted is He, singled out the people of knowledge so that it would be easy for them to leave aside what they are known for being eager for, namely the elevation of assemblies and their love for being at the front. This is one of the unseen matters of the Qur'an, since rivalry in this matter has appeared from these people in every age.

Al-Khafaji included this in quoting the words of the author of al-Intisaf, but his statement, as you have heard it, is more fitting to etiquette with people of knowledge. I do not think that "those who have been given knowledge" mentioned in the verse are like the scholars whom al-Khafaji alluded to. Yes, he, may Allah have mercy on him, is truthful in what he said regarding many scholars of the last age, such as the scholars of his time and the scholars of our time. But for many of these, applying the title "scholar" to one of them is a metaphor whose relation is not known, and despite this his heart is filled with love of the front seats and he competes with the true scholars, not realizing where he would truly stand if he were fair with his incapacity. This is what I say. Some scholars have used the verse to argue for giving precedence to knowledge, even a young man from the Banu Bahila over an ignorant person, even if he is an old man from the Banu Hashim. This is based on what was mentioned before about its meaning, because it indicates the virtue of the knowledgeable person over other believers, and that Allah raises him over them on the Day of Resurrection, and makes his rank above theirs. So his place in the gatherings of this world should be above the place of the ignorant person.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said in the book al-Ahkam: "Some people said: the meaning of the verse is that Allah, exalted is He, raises the believing scholars among you by degrees above others. Therefore He commanded making room for them. In this there is evidence for raising scholars in gatherings and making room for them away from the high places." End.

This meaning that he reported is evident in that the two conjoined items are one in essence, and the conjunction serves to make the difference of attributes equivalent to the difference of essence. This is a remote possibility. It also appears from it that he thought that يَرْفَعْ (yarfa') is in the nominative, on the basis that the sentence is a resumptive clause (istinaf) that came as an answer to the question about the reason for the preceding command. However, the matter is not like that. It is possible that he knew that it is in the jussive (majzum) as the response to the command, but he did not consider that the raising (rafʿ) being "degrees" is its reward, in the manner in which the making of room (al-fasḥ) before it is its reward. So reflect on it.

﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ This is a warning to whoever does not comply with the command and is averse to it.

It was also read as بِما يَعْمَلُونَ, with the letter ya' (بِالياءِ التَّحْتانِيَّةِ), i.e., the verb in the third person plural.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 58, verse 12:

﴿O you who have believed, when you consult the Messenger privately﴾, meaning: when you wish to confer privately with him, upon him be blessings and peace, about some matter of the affairs. ﴿Then precede your private consultation with a charity﴾, meaning: give charity before it. In the phrase there is a figurative allegory (istiʿarah tamthiliyyah), and the original construction is used of one who has two hands. The private consultation is likened to a person, and attributing two hands to it is an imaginative representation (takhyil). Regarding "bayna" (between), it is said to be a supporting term (tarshih), and its meaning is "before." In this command there is the honouring of the Messenger (ﷺ), benefit for the poor, a distinction between the sincere believer and the hypocrite, and between one who loves the Hereafter and one who loves this world, and a restraint on crowding in upon him (ﷺ) without an important need. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah that a group of Muslims often conferred privately with the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, without a real need, only so that their station would be displayed. He (ﷺ) was generous and would not turn anyone away, so this verse was revealed.

It is related from Muqatil that the wealthy used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and engage him in private conversation often, and they would overwhelm the poor in the gatherings, until he, upon him be blessings and peace, disliked their long sitting and private conversation, so this was revealed. There is a difference of opinion over whether the command is one of recommendation (nadb) or obligation (jawab), but it was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿Are you apprehensive...?﴾ etc. Although that is connected to it in recitation, it is not connected to it in revelation. It is also said that it was abrogated by the verse of zakat. The reliable view is the first. The amount of the charity was not specified, so that both much and little would suffice.

At-Tirmidhi related it and graded it good, along with a group of others, from ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿O you who have believed, when you consult...﴾ etc., the Prophet (ﷺ) said to me: 'What do you think of a dinar?' I said: 'They cannot bear it.' He said: 'Half a dinar?' I said: 'They cannot bear it.' He said: 'Then how much?' I said: 'A barley-grain.' He said: 'Indeed you are of little renunciation.'" Then when ﴿Are you apprehensive...?﴾ was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God has lightened this for this community." According to the well-known view, no one other than him, may God ennoble his face, acted upon it.

Al-Hakim related it and graded it sound, and Ibn al-Mundhir, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and others related from him, may God ennoble his face, that he said: "Indeed in the Book of God there is a verse that no one acted upon before me and no one will act upon after me: the verse of private consultation, ﴿O you who have believed, when you consult the Messenger...﴾ etc. I had a dinar, so I sold it for ten dirhams, and whenever I conferred privately with the Prophet (ﷺ) I would precede my private consultation with a dirham. Then it was abrogated, so no one acted upon it, and there was revealed ﴿Are you apprehensive...?﴾ the verse." It is said: this, according to the view that it is obligatory, is to be understood as meaning that the wealthy did not happen to have a private consultation during the period the ruling remained in force. The duration of its remaining in force was disputed: according to Muqatil it was ten nights, and Qatadah said it was an hour of the day. It is also said that it was abrogated before it was acted upon, but this is not sound, because of what has been authenticated just above.

It is recited as "ṣadaqāt" (charities) in the plural, in keeping with the plural of the addressees. ﴿That﴾, meaning the precedence of charities, ﴿is better for you﴾, because of the reward in it, ﴿and purer﴾ and more pure for your souls, because in it there is training them to be unconcerned with wealth and weakening the bond of its love, which defiles them. In this there is an indication that in it there is a preparation of the soul for greater benefit from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) during private consultation.

In the passage there is an indication of the recommendation (nadb) of precedence of charity. But His saying: ﴿But if you do not find [the means], then indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: for whoever does not find it, since He, glorified is He, granted him permission for private consultation without precedence of charity, is more indicative of obligation.

﴿Are you apprehensive that you will offer charity before your private consultation?﴾ That is, "Did you fear poverty on account of offering charity?" The object of *ashfaqtum* (you feared) is therefore omitted, and *an* (أنْ, "that") is governed by an implied *harf al-ta'lil* (particle of causation, "because of"). It is also permissible for the object to be ﴿that you offer﴾ itself, with no omission, meaning: "Did you fear offering charity, lest poverty be the consequence of it?" The word *sadaqat* (charities) is in the plural because the fear was not in reality of offering a single charity, since a single charity is not a likely cause of poverty. Rather, the fear was of the continuation of the matter. The plural *sadaqat* is more apt than the view that the plural corresponds to the plural of the addressees. From the plural it is known why *sadaqah* (charity) appears in the singular in what precedes, according to the recitation of the majority (*qira'at al-Jumhur*, the widely transmitted reading).

﴿So when you did not do it﴾, namely what you were commanded and what was difficult for you, ﴿and God turned to you [in forgiveness]﴾, by permitting you to consult in private without offering charity. In this, according to what has been said, is an indication that their apprehension was a sin which God overlooked, because of what was seen of their compliance and their lack of fear of poverty after what had taken the place of their repentance. *Idh* (إذ) remains in its original sense, namely that it is an adverb of time (*zarf*) referring to the past. It has also been said that it has the meaning of the temporal *idh* referring to the future, as in His saying: ﴿when the shackles are around their necks﴾ [Ghafir: 71].

It has also been said that it has the meaning of the conditional *in* (إنِ), as if it were said: "If you do not do it, then ﴿establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾." The meaning according to the first view is: you neglected that in the past, so make up for it by persevering in establishing the prayer and giving zakat. Perseverance is considered because those addressed are already establishing prayer and paying zakat. He departed from *fa-salu* (فَصَلُّوا, "then pray") to ﴿fa-aqimu al-salah﴾ (فَأقِيمُوا الصَّلاةَ, "then establish the prayer") so that what is meant is persistence in fulfilling the rights of the prayer and observing what is required of it in its full form, not merely the bare performance of the act. Since he departed from that for the reason mentioned, what follows was brought in the same pattern and He did not say *wa-zakku* (وزَكُّوا, "and purify yourselves") lest it be supposed that the intended meaning is a command to purify the self. Thus it has been said; so reflect.

﴿And obey God and His Messenger﴾, that is, in all the other commands, among them what has preceded within His saying: ﴿O you who believe, when you are told to make room in the assemblies, then make room﴾ and the verses that follow, and other than that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 58, verse 14:

﴿Have you not seen﴾ is an expression of wonder at the state of the hypocrites (munafiqun), who used to take the Jews as allies (awliya', sing. wali), give them sincere counsel, and convey to them the secrets of the believers. It is said, as al-Khafaji stated, that there is here a shift in address (talwin al-khitab), turning the address away from the believers toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: "Have you not looked at" ﴿those who took as allies﴾, that is, who befriended ﴿a people with whom Allah is angry﴾, and they are the Jews, ﴿they are not of you﴾, that is, those who took them as allies are not of you, O company of believers, ﴿nor of them﴾, that is, not of those people upon whom Allah is angry, namely the Jews, because they are hypocrites, wavering between that (mudhabdhabun bayna dhalik). In a hadith: "The likeness of the hypocrite is the likeness of a goat wandering between two flocks" — that is, one that wavers between two herds, not knowing which one to follow.

Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that "they" (hum) refers to the people, and the pronoun in "minhum" refers to those who took them as allies. Then he said: "In that case, the act of the hypocrites is baser, because they took as allies people upon whom Allah is angry, who are not of their own kind, so they do not owe them protection (dhimam), nor are they of the righteous people, so that alliance would be correct."

The first reading is the apparent one, and the sentence according to it is independent (mustanafa'a). It was also permitted that the sentence be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿they took as allies﴾; it was objected that it lacks a waw, and it was answered that they have stated that a nominal sentence, affirmative or negative, when it occurs as a circumstantial clause, comes with the waw alone, with the pronoun alone, or with both together. What occurs here comes with the pronoun alone, namely "hum." According to what Ibn 'Atiyya said, it is in the position of an attribute (sifa) for "qawm" (a people).

Al-Mawla Sa'd Allah mentioned that in ﴿minkum﴾ there is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person). It was rebutted that if the address of the Messenger (ﷺ) is predominant in it, then clearly there is no iltifat in it; and if it is not predominant, then likewise there is no iltifat in it, since it does not contradict the requirement of the apparent sense, given that their address preceded it. As for considering it an iltifat according to the view of al-Sakkaki, there is room for scrutiny. ﴿And they swear falsely by Allah﴾ is a conjunction with ﴿they took as allies﴾, falling within the scope of the wonder. It was also permitted that it be conjoined to the clause ﴿they are not of you﴾. The present tense form indicates the repetition of the oath. And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿while they know﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "they swear," conveying the complete abomination of what they did, for swearing to what one knows to be false is extremely vile. It has been used as evidence that lying (kadhib) covers both what the speaker knows corresponds to reality and what he does not know corresponds to it. This is refuted by it according to the views of al-Nazzam and al-Jahiz, since according to them there is no need for it. It was examined in this respect that it is possible that by "lying" is meant what contradicts their belief, and ﴿while they know﴾ means "while they know its opposite," so it would be a circumstantial clause that is emphatic (mu'akkida), not restrictive (muqayyada). Indeed, the establishing (ta'sis) is the original, but it is not fixed, and the possibility invalidates the inference. The lie by which they swore was their claim to Islam in reality. It has also been said: they did not revile the Prophet (ﷺ), based on what has been narrated: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting in the shade of one of his chambers, and with him was a group of Muslims. He said: 'There will come to you a man who looks at you with the eyes of a devil; when he comes, do not speak to him.' They had not waited long when a blue-eyed man came upon them. The Prophet (ﷺ), when he saw him, said: 'Why do you and your companions revile me?' He said: 'Leave me, and I will bring them to you.' He went off, called them, and they swore," and then the verse was revealed. This hadith was reported by Imam Ahmad, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, from Ibn 'Abbas, except that its end is: "Then Allah revealed: ﴿On the day when Allah resurrects them all, and they swear to Him as they swear to you﴾ [al-Mujadila: 18]," and the verse that follows it. Perhaps it also supports the consideration that the lie is their claim that they did not revile.

In al-Bahr there is a narration similar to this from al-Suddi and Muqatil, which is: "He (ﷺ) said to his companions: 'There will enter upon you a man whose heart is the heart of a tyrant, and who looks with the eyes of a devil.' 'Abd Allah ibn Nabtal entered, and he was blue-eyed, dark-skinned, with a thin beard. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Why do you and your companions revile me?' He swore by Allah that he had not done it. He said to him: 'You did.' He brought his companions, and they swore by Allah that they had not reviled him," and then the verse was revealed. Allah knows best its authenticity. This 'Abd Allah is the man left unnamed in the first report. He is the son of Nabtal (with a fatha on the nun, sukun on the ba' with a single dot, followed by a taa' with two dots above and a lam), son of al-Harith ibn Qays al-Ansari al-Awsi. Ibn al-Kalbi and al-Baladhuri mentioned him among the hypocrites, while Abu 'Ubayda mentioned him among the Companions. It is possible, as Ibn Hajar said, that he came to know that he had repented. As for the statement in the Qamus: "'Abd Allah ibn Nabil (like Amir), among the hypocrites," it is possible that he is this same man, and the name of his father has been differently vocalized; it is also possible that he is someone else.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 58, verse 15:

﴿Allah has prepared for them﴾ because of that ﴿a severe punishment﴾, a kind of punishment that is increasingly intense. ﴿Indeed, evil is what they have been doing﴾, that which they had become accustomed to doing and had trained themselves in.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 58, verse 16:

﴿They have taken their oaths﴾ — the false oaths by which they swear when there is need — ﴿as a shield﴾: a protection and a cover against being called to account. Al-Alusi quotes from al-Irshad (Abu al-Su'ud's commentary): "Taking (ittikhadh) on this reading is an expression for concealing oneself by action, as if it were said: they concealed themselves behind the faith they displayed, so that their blood and property would not be made lawful." On the reading of the majority (of reciters), it is an expression for their preparing their false oaths and readying them until the time of need, so that they might swear by them and escape being called to account, not for actually using them, for that comes after being called to account, which is preceded by the commission of the crime, and also after its cause, as the particle "fa" (then) in His words, ﴿so they barred﴾, indicates; that is, they barred people.

﴿from the way of Allah﴾ — in the midst of their safety, by discouraging those they met from entering Islam and by weakening the affair of the Muslims in their eyes. It has also been said: they barred the Muslims from killing them, for that is the way of Allah concerning them. It has also been said: "ṣaddū" is intransitive, and the meaning is that they turned away from Islam in reality; and this, as you see, is far-fetched. ﴿For them is a humiliating punishment﴾ — a second threat, with a different description of their punishment. It has been said: the first is the punishment of the grave, and this is the punishment of the Hereafter; its description as "humiliating," which requires manifestness, supports this, so there is no repetition.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 58, verse 18:

﴿On the day when Allah raises them all up together﴾. The discussion of its like has already preceded, not far back. ﴿Then they swear to Him﴾, that is, to Allah, the Exalted, on that day, saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. ﴿As they swear to you﴾ in the world, that they are Muslims like you. The comparison is merely with the act of swearing to them in the world, even though the object sworn upon differs, based on what we have mentioned earlier regarding the occasion of revelation. ﴿And they think﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿that they﴾, by these wicked oaths, ﴿are upon something﴾ of bringing about a benefit or repelling a harm, just as they were upon it in the world, where they would use them to protect their lives and their wealth and to draw worldly advantages. ﴿Verily, they are the liars﴾, those who have gone to an extreme in lying beyond which there is no further extreme, in that they dared to lie in the presence of the Knower of the unseen, and they supposed that their wicked oaths would make their lie current with Him, Mighty and Majestic, just as it is current with the believers.

﴿The Shaytan has gained mastery over them﴾, meaning he overcame their minds through his whispering and his embellishing, until they followed him, so he became dominant over them. Al-Raghib said: al-hawdh is that the driver follows the hind part of the camel, i.e. the rear of its two thighs, and so it is harshly urged on in its driving. It is said: haadha al-ibila yahuduha, meaning he drove the camels with a harsh driving. The saying of the Exalted: ﴿The Shaytan has gained mastery over them﴾ means he drove them while dominating them, or it derives from their saying: istahwadha al-'ir 'ala al-atan, meaning the male donkey mastered the she-donkey, i.e. he came to be over her hawdh, that is, the two sides of her back. End of quotation.

Some eminent scholars stated that al-hawdh originally means driving and gathering. In the Qamus, driving is restricted to swift driving, and then it was applied to taking control. Similar to it are al-ahwadh and al-ahwadhi, which, as al-Asma'i said, means one who is energetic in affairs and dominant over them, from whom nothing escapes. From this is the saying of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with them both, about Umar: "He was ahwadhi, unique in himself," which is derived from this. As for istahwadha, it is among the forms that retain their original root without i'lal (vowel-change for ease of pronunciation) contrary to analogy (qiyas, the regular pattern). Analogically it should be istahadha, with the waw converted to alif, as has been heard rarely. Abu 'Amr recited it this way here, so it comes contrary to analogy, like istanwaqa and istasawaba, although its usage is the well-known one. For this reason its usage does not detract from its eloquence. In the form istaf'ala here there is an intensification that is not in the form of ﴿So He caused them to forget the remembrance of Allah﴾, meaning He did not enable them to remember Him, the Mighty and Majestic, because of the desires He made attractive to them. Hence they do not remember Him at all, neither with their hearts nor with their tongues. ﴿Those﴾, described with what has been mentioned of vices, ﴿are the party of the Shaytan﴾, i.e. his soldiers and followers.

﴿Unquestionably, the party of the Shaytan are the losers﴾, i.e. those described with a loss that has no end beyond it, since they forfeited for themselves everlasting bliss and took instead painful punishment. In opening the sentence with the two particles of alerting and affirmation, and in stating the two correlatives explicitly in a place where a pronoun would be expected in one of the two ways, and in inserting the separating pronoun, there are forms of emphasis that are not hidden.

Surah 58, verse 20 — Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani):

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 58, verse 21:

﴿Allah has decreed﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that gives the reason why they are among the most humiliated. That is, He recorded it in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or He decreed and judged it. From Qatadah, he said: "Whichever it is, it takes the place of an oath. Glorified is He destroyed many of their enemies with various kinds of punishment, such as the people of Noah, the people of Salih, the people of Lot, and others. The war between our Prophet (ﷺ) and the polytheists, although it was in alternation (sijal), the final outcome was in his favour, peace be upon him. Likewise for his followers after them, but only if their struggle against the enemies of the religion is like the struggle of the messengers against them, in that it is sincerely for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and not for seeking kingship, power, or worldly aims. Then you will hardly find a fighter of this kind who is not, in general, victorious. Some scholars restricted victory to argument alone, not to its continuous pursuit, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) makes it unlikely. **Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 58, verse 22:**

﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾. This is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. The verb *tajid* ("you find") is either transitive to two objects, in which case His saying ﴿loving﴾ (*yuwaddduna*) and what follows is its second object, or transitive to one object, in which case the phrase is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from its object, because the object is specified by the description. It has been said that it is another description of it, meaning "a people who combine belief in Allah the Exalted and the Last Day with loving the enemies of Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ)." But this is not the right reading. According to what is in al-Kashshaf, the statement is of the type of *takhyil* (imaginative depiction): it is imagined that it is impossible and inconceivable to find a people who are believers and yet ﴿love﴾ the polytheists. The purpose of this is that such a thing should not be, and that it should be rejected and should not be found in any way. This is an exaggeration in forbidding it, in warning against involvement in it, and in insisting on keeping away from the enemies of Allah the Exalted. The essence of this, according to al-Kashf, is that it is from the supposition of something that does not exist as though it existed in reality: the negation of finding is stated with respect to the attribute, while what is meant is the negation of its being appropriate (*inbighā'*) to find such people with that attribute. So the negation of appropriateness was made into the negation of finding. What actually occurs is the negation of appropriateness, but it was imagined that the negation of finding is what occurs. Thus the depiction lies in making what is not impossible into something impossible.

It has been said that what is meant is: you will not find a people who have perfect faith in this state. Then the negation remains on its literal meaning. What is meant by loving those who oppose Allah is supporting them and backing them. The present tense (*mudari'*) has been said to be used to narrate a past state. The phrase ﴿those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾ is clearly about the disbeliever, while some reports indicate that it includes the depraved sinner (*fasiq*). The reports explicitly prohibit allying with depraved sinners as with polytheists. Indeed, Sufyan said: "They see that this verse was revealed concerning those who mix with rulers."

In a lengthy hadith recorded by al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and al-Tirmidhi from Wathila ibn al-Asqa', raised (to the Prophet): "Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: 'By My might, My mercy will not reach whoever does not ally with My friends and show enmity to My enemies.'"

Ahmad and others recorded from al-Bara' ibn Azib, raised: "The firmest of faith is love for the sake of Allah and hatred for the sake of Allah."

Al-Daylami recorded through al-Hasan from Mu'adh, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, do not make for a wicked person – and in another narration – or a depraved sinner any hand or favour upon me, so that my heart would love him. For I have found in what You revealed to me: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾."

Al-Kawashi related from Sahl that he said: Whoever has made his faith sound and purified his monotheism will not be familiar with an innovator (*mubtadi'*), will not sit with him, eat with him, drink with him, or keep his company, and will show him enmity and hatred from himself. Whoever flatters an innovator, Allah the Exalted will deprive him of the sweetness of the Sunnah. Whoever seeks affection from an innovator, desiring the honour of this world or some worldly benefit, Allah the Exalted will humble him by that very honour and make him poor by that very wealth. Whoever laughs with an innovator, Allah the Exalted will pull the light of faith out of his heart. Whoever does not believe this, let him test it. End of quotation.

It is strange that some who claim affiliation with the Sufis – and they are not of them, not even a paring of a fingernail – ally with the oppressors, and indeed with those who have no connection to religion at all, and support them falsely, and display such love for them that the page cannot contain its explanation. When the verses of Allah the Exalted and the hadiths of His Messenger (ﷺ) which forbid such things are recited to him, he says: "I will treat my heart by reading about two pages of the noble Mathnawi of our master Jalal al-Din al-Qunawi – may his secret be sanctified and his darkness, if any, be removed – through the lights I receive while reading it." By my life, this is the far error. It is incumbent upon believers to avoid such people.

﴿Even if they were﴾, that is, those who oppose Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him), the plural is used in view of the meaning of *man* (whoever), just as the singular was used earlier in view of its wording. ﴿Their fathers﴾, that is, those they love, ﴿or their sons, or their brothers, or their kindred﴾. For it is a requirement of faith in Allah the Exalted and the Last Day, on which a person will be gathered together with whom he loved, that they should entirely abandon all of them. The intended meaning is not these specific persons, but relatives in general. He mentioned fathers first because it is obligatory for their sons to obey them and to keep them company in this world kindly. He mentioned sons second because they are closest to them, being their livers (*akbad*, i.e., dearest parts). He mentioned brothers third because they are the helpers of one another. As the poet said:

*Your brother, your brother, for whoever has no brother
is like one who runs to battle without a weapon.*

He ended with the kindred because reliance upon them and mutual support with them comes generally after brothers. As another poet said:

*Had I been of Mazin, my camels would not have been plundered,
the sons of al-Laqita of Dhuhl ibn Shaiban*

*then there would have risen to support me a rough folk,
in time of anger, even if a man of wounds were to stand up.*

*They do not ask their brother when he calls them
in calamities, for the proof he has given.*

Abu Raja' read *wa 'asha'iratahum* ("and their clans") in the plural. ﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those whom they do not love, even if they are the closest people to them and most closely related to them. The sense of distance (in the demonstrative) is for the elevation of their rank in virtue. ﴿Those﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*), whose predicate is His saying: ﴿He has written faith into their hearts﴾, that is, Allah the Exalted has established it in them. Since a thing is intended first, then said, then written, the statement expresses the origin in terms of the endpoint, for emphasis and exaggeration. In this there is evidence that deeds are excluded from the concept of faith (*iman*), since a part of what is firmly established in the heart is certainly established in it, and nothing from the deeds of the limbs is established in the heart.

Abu Haywa and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read *kutiba* in the passive voice, with *al-iman* ("faith") in the nominative as its deputy subject.

﴿And He strengthened them﴾, that is, supported them ﴿with a spirit from Himself﴾, that is, from Him, Mighty and Majestic, with *min* being for origin. By "spirit" is meant the light of the heart, a light that Allah the Exalted casts into the heart of whoever of His servants He wills, through which tranquillity is attained and one ascends the stages of realisation. Calling it "spirit" is a figurative metonymy (*majaz mursal*), because it is the cause of a good and eternal life. It has been permitted that it be a metaphor (*isti'ara*); the statement of some eminent scholars, that the light of the heart is what the physicians have called "spirit", namely the subtle ray formed from the heart – by which perception occurs – is, in its literal sense, nothing, as is not hidden. Or what is meant by it is the Qur'an, according to the two previous possibilities, and the metaphor is preferred; or it is Gabriel (peace be upon him), and that was on the day of Badr. The application of "spirit" to him is a widespread usage.

It has been said that the pronoun in ﴿from Him﴾ refers to faith, and the spirit also means faith, and the statement is an instance of *tajrid badi'i* (a rhetorical figure of abstraction). Then *min* is explanatory (*bayaniyya*) or for origin, according to the disagreement about it. The application of "spirit" to faith is as previously explained.

His saying: ﴿And He will admit them﴾ to the end is an explanation of the effects of His mercy in the Hereafter after the explanation of His worldly kindnesses, that is, and He will admit them into the Hereafter.

﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾, forever and ever. His saying: ﴿Allah is pleased with them﴾ is a resumptive clause functioning as a reason for what He has bestowed upon them of the effects of His mercy, Mighty and Majestic, in this world and the next. His saying ﴿and they are pleased with Him﴾ explains their joy in what they were given, both in this world and the next. His saying: ﴿Those are the party of Allah﴾ is an honouring of them by explaining their special relationship with Him, the Exalted. His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Surely the party of Allah are the successful﴾ explains their special share of the happiness of both abodes. The discussion of the embellishment of the sentence with *ala* ("surely") and *inna* ("indeed") is as previously explained regarding similar cases. It has been said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him.

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Juraij, who said: "It was related to me that Abu Quhafa insulted the Prophet (ﷺ), so Abu Bakr slapped him, and he fell. This was mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'Did you do that, O Abu Bakr?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do not do it again.' He said: 'By Allah, if the sword were near me, I would strike him.' – and in another narration – 'I would kill him.' Then the verses ﴿You will not find a people...﴾ were revealed."

It has also been said that it was revealed concerning Abu 'Ubayda ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Jarrah. Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilya*, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* recorded from Ibn 'Abbas, from 'Abd Allah ibn Shawdhab, who said: "The father of Abu 'Ubayda kept challenging him on the day of Badr, and Abu 'Ubayda kept avoiding him. When he persisted, Abu 'Ubayda went for him and killed him, and then ﴿You will not find...﴾ was revealed." In al-Kashshaf it is said that Abu 'Ubayda killed his father 'Abd Allah ibn al-Jarrah on the day of Uhud. Al-Waqidi, regarding the story of his killing him, said: "So say the people of Syria. I have asked men from Banu Fihr, and they said: 'His father died before Islam,' that is, in the Jahiliyya, before the appearance of Islam." End of quotation.

The truth is that he killed him at Badr. Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded from Anas, who said: "Abu 'Ubayda had killed his father with his own hand, and he was among the prisoners of Badr, when he heard from him something about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he disliked, and he forbade him, but he did not desist." It has been said that the verse was revealed concerning him when he killed his father.

And concerning Abu Bakr: on the day of Badr he called his son to single combat, and said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Let me be in the first *ra'la*" – that is, the first detachment of horsemen. He said: "Enjoy yourself with your own self, O Abu Bakr. Do you not know that you are with me as my hearing and my sight?" Concerning Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, he killed his brother 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr on the day of Uhud. Concerning 'Umar, he killed his maternal uncle al-'As ibn Hisham on the day of Badr. Concerning 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Hamza and 'Ubayda ibn al-Harith, they killed 'Utba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabi'a, and al-Walid ibn 'Utba on the day of Badr.

The detail of this is what Abu Dawud recorded from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "When the day of Badr came, 'Utba ibn Rabi'a advanced, with his son and his brother, and called out: 'Who will duel?' ... Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Stand up, O Hamza! Stand up, O 'Ali! Stand up, O 'Ubayda ibn al-Harith!' So Hamza came to 'Utba, I came to Shayba, and between 'Ubayda and al-Walid there was an exchange of two blows, each of them wounding the other. Then we turned upon al-Walid, killed him, and carried 'Ubayda away."

Some exegetes have arranged ﴿even if they were their fathers, or their sons, or their brothers, or their kindred﴾ according to the story of Abu 'Ubayda, Abu Bakr, Mus'ab, 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and those with them. It has also been said that His saying ﴿You will not find a people...﴾ to the end was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a. The apparent view, as has been said, is that it is connected to the verses concerning the hypocrites who allied with the Jews. Whatever the case, the ruling of the verses is general, even if they were revealed concerning particular persons, as is not hidden. And Allah knows best.
